The purpose of this report was
to present the Buckinghamshire Youth Justice Plan 2026 –
2029, as set out in the appendix. The Youth Justice Plan provided
details of progress made against statutory outcomes for children
and victims. It outlined priorities for the next 3 years, alongside
potential future challenges for the partnership.
 
The plan had been developed in
collaboration with children, parents/carers and victims supported
by the service. The plan demonstrated the strength of practice,
commitment and approach from the service alongside the partnership
which had supported to achieve strong outcome measures against
National Indicators and supported to improve the lives of children,
families and victims.

Youth Justice Planbe endorsed and
recommended to Council for adoption.

purpose:
Each Director of Public Health in England is
required to produce a statutory annual report on the health of
their population.  This year's report is titled
'Buckinghamshire’s Building Blocks: A Blueprint for Better
Health & Wellbeing'.
content:
Each Director of Public Health in England is
required to produce a statutory annual report on the health of
their population.  This year's report is titled
'Buckinghamshire’s Building Blocks: A Blueprint for Better
Health & Wellbeing'.

Each year every Director of Public Health in
England must produce a statutory annual report on the health of
their population.
 
Buckinghamshire Director of Public Health
Annual Report (DPHAR) 2026 focussed on the theme of the Building
Blocks of Health, and these related to a range of teams and
services across the Council, and partner organisations. This theme
built on last year’s Annual Report entitled
‘Tomorrow’s World- health and wellbeing in
Buckinghamshire in 2045’ by outlining more on how ill-health
could be prevented and how to secure a healthier and more
prosperous Buckinghamshire in the future.
 
This report aimed to reframe our understanding
of health and the key factors that determine it. It explored seven
different ‘Building Blocks’, how these impacted the
residents of Buckinghamshire and what could be done collectively to
improve the health and wellbeing of Buckinghamshire
residents. 
 
The recommendations from the report were broad
and did not only sit with Buckinghamshire Council, but required the
input of several different organisations, often working together in
partnership.
 
RESOLVED that the Director of Public Health Annual Report 2026
be noted and endorsed.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Director of Public Health Annual Report 2026 for Buckinghamshire, focusing on improving health and wellbeing in the region.

purpose:
Update of the Bucks Better Lives Strategy
informing people of how they should expect to receive services
content:
Update of the Bucks Better Lives Strategy
informing people of how they should expect to receive services

The Council’s Better
Lives strategy was as relevant today as it was when first
introduced in 2018. It provided a consistent and person-centred
framework for enabling people to live at home and as independently
as long as possible. Enabling people to stay independent delivered
better outcomes, improved wellbeing, reduced the need for long term
care, and supported a sustainable service model for the
future.
 
The strategy had been updated
and built on this strong foundation, setting out the
Council’s vision for a future where all residents were
empowered to live well in their communities with minimal reliance
on long term support. People would experience care that was planned
around individual need across health and social care services,
would have greater choice and control, and would benefit from
strong community networks.
 
The Better Lives Strategy was
structured around three core pillars that underpinned all the
work:
·      
Living Independently - supporting people to access
the right information, advice and community networks to stay well
for longer.
·      
Regaining Independence - providing timely,
practical, short-term support that helped people recover skills and
return home safely following illness, injury or a change in
circumstances.
·      
Living with Support - ensuring people who needed
longer term care received personalised, high-quality support that
promoted choice, control and dignity, with strong recognition of
the vital role played by carers.
 
The current version of the
Better Lives Strategy was adopted by Cabinet in January 2022.
Following review, the strategy had been updated to reflect changes
in the national and local policy context. There were no substantive
changes to the approach and three pillar model. The updates
included more detail on how the Council commissioned for better
lives, supported the workforce and evidenced impact. An action plan
was in place to support delivery and would be updated
annually.
 
RESOLVED that the Better Lives Strategy 2026 – 2031 be
approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Better Lives Strategy 2026 - 2031, aiming to empower residents to live well in their communities with minimal reliance on long term support.

purpose: Quarterly report
content:
This report set out the recommended updates to
the Council’s Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2029/30 since
the approval of the budget by Full Council in February 2026.
 
The Council’s Capital Programme for
2026/27 to 2029/30 was approved by Full Council in February 2026,
totalling £628.272m. Since then, there had been slippage of
£18.163m (10.4%) in 25-26 which would roll forward in the
programme, and new funding had been announced by Government to be
added to the Programme. In addition, through the closing of the
accounts for 25/26, some projects had now completed with unspent
funding, to be removed from the programme, and small number of
projects overspent and required funding from contingency.
 
The revised Capital Programme for 2026/27 to
2029/30 totalled £655.542m. Services had reviewed the profile
of expected spend in 26/27 and had reprofiled the programme to
align it with their updated delivery plans.
 
This report detailed those changes for
recommendation to Cabinet. The recommendations in this report
complied with the Capital Gateway Process.
 
RESOLVED that the
recommended changes to the Capital Programme be approved:
1.     
£10.794m of additions to the Capital Programme, which are
funded from ringfenced grants and s.106 as set out in section 2 of
the report.
2.     
£4.116m of removals due to completion or underspend of
ringfenced-funded projects, as set out in section 3 of the
report.
3.     
The transfer of £0.037m of underspends on corporately
funded projects to the capital contingency, as set out in section 4
of the report.
4.     
The release of £0.115m from the capital contingency as a
technical adjustment to fund overspends in 25-26, as set out in
section 5 of the report.
5.     
The reprofile of £30.707m from 2026/27 into future years
as set out in section 6 of the report.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommended updates to the Council's Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2029/30.

purpose: Quarterly report
content:
This report set out the forecast Revenue and
Capital outturn position for Buckinghamshire Council for the
financial year 2026/27 as at Quarter 1. Overall, the forecast
revenue outturn was a balanced position.
 
The Council continued to experience pressures
from increases in demand and complexity of need in the key services
of Adult Social Care, Children’s Social Care, Temporary
Accommodation, and High Needs budgets within the Dedicated Schools
Grant (DSG).
 
Portfolios were reporting an adverse variance
of £4.9m (1.0% of Portfolio budgets), offset by a favourable
variance in Corporate and Funding budgets.
 
There were pressures within Children’s
Social Care of £6.7m linked to cost and complexity of Looked
After Children and challenges in the delivery of planned MTFP
savings; in Adult Social Care £2.0m and Temporary
Accommodation £0.4m. These pressures were offset by the
expected growth in Home to School Transport not coming through as
quickly as projected and additional income within planning.
 
A balanced position overall was due to a
favourable variance in Corporate and Funding budgets. This had
created the opportunity to make some one-off investments and
included an allowance of £10.1m to be set aside for risk in
the context of the current geopolitical climate and for investment
in key priorities.
 
Cabinet was recommended to approve the
following one-off investments:

·      
Reallocate £3m of the in-year growth in Home to School
Transport into Children’s Services to continue the
improvement journey across the Council from ‘good’ to
‘great’. This investment would allow the Council to
embed data, system, service user, and process improvements, to be
sustainable and efficient, enabling the Council to deliver the
streamlined services which supported the Children’s Services
reform programmes and positive outcomes for children and young
people.

·      
Invest £2.2m in Regeneration programme in Leader portfolio to
accelerate investment in the Town Centres.
 
The Dedicated Schools Grant budget had been
set with a deficit of £30.3m. Currently the forecast position
was £0.2m above budget. There was an improved position on the
DSG deficit reserve, following a review of the 2025/26 outturn
undertaken with DfE advisors in June relating to Early Years
funding. The opening balance on the DSG deficit reserve was now
£42.8m with a forecast closing balance of £73.3m. It
was assumed that 90% of this deficit would be funded from the High
Needs Sustainability grant.
 
The forecast position on capital budgets was
£191.0m, which broadly matched the current budget after
reprofiling to reflect an updated and prudent view on the delivery
of projects.
 
The budget included an approved savings
programme of £128m over 3 years across General Fund and DSG,
with £61.4m to be delivered in 2026/27. Delivery of savings
for 2026/27 was currently below target due to challenges in
Education and Children’s Services. Strong action was being
taken to drive forward our successful savings programmes.
 
The report contained recommendations to update
Fees & Charges which were set out in detail at Appendix 3.
These related to minor amendments and clarifications on the Fees
& Charges previously published in January 2026.
 
The report included updates to the budgets for
Grants, which were set out in detail at Appendix 4. These related
to variations in ring-fenced grants since the Budget was set in
February 2026.
 
RESOLVED

       
i.           
That the report and the balanced revenue position
be noted.

     
ii.           
That the forecast capital outturn position of
£191.0m of investment in the Council’s priorities be
noted.

   
iii.           
That the investment proposals as set out in
paragraph 1.6 of the report be approved.

   
iv.           
That the changes to Fees and Charges in Appendix
3 be approved.

     
v.           
That the budget changes for Grants in Appendix 4
be approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve one-off investments and budget updates for Buckinghamshire Council for the financial year 2026/27.

purpose:
Seeking approval of funding from the
Buckinghamshire Growth Fund
content:
The Council developed and
launched an investment programme called the Buckinghamshire Growth
Fund, which went live in March 2026 with its first call for
projects. In broad terms the fund supports Economic Development
within the county through programmes and activities that enhance
the delivery of the Economic Growth Plan, regeneration ambitions
and accelerate the growth and development of the Buckinghamshire
Enterprise Zones.
 
Prior to the launch of the
fund, the Council was aware of two major investment propositions,
which had already developed a full business case and were at
critical point of seeking additional funding to secure the status
of the projects.
 
Buckinghamshire Council had a
unique opportunity to support these two strategically significant,
investment-ready projects that directly align with the
Buckinghamshire Economic Growth Plan and the objectives of the
Buckinghamshire Growth Fund. Full business cases had been submitted
for both the National Autonomy & Drone Innovation Centre
(NADIC) at Westcott and the Robert Bosch Centre for Innovation
& Excellence at Denham, placing them at a more advanced stage
of development than other emerging propositions from the recent
investment proposal call.
 
Both projects were well
positioned to contribute to Buckinghamshire’s ambitions to
grow high-value sectors, foster innovation, strengthen business
collaboration, develop future skills, and enhance the
county’s reputation as a location for research, technology
and advanced industry investment. Their advanced status, coupled
with time-sensitive match-funding requirements, creates a strong
case for prioritised investment decisions.
 
The National Autonomy &
Drone Innovation Centre (NADIC) would strengthen
Buckinghamshire’s unique position within the rapidly growing
autonomous systems, aerospace and drone technology sectors. The
project was expected to support innovation, attract high-value
businesses and investment, create skilled employment opportunities,
and provide a platform for collaboration between industry, academia
and government partners. Investment in NADIC would reinforce the
strategic importance of the Westcott Enterprise Zone and support
the county’s long-term productivity and competitiveness
objectives.
 
The Robert Bosch Centre for
Innovation & Excellence represented a significant opportunity
to secure private-sector-led research, innovation and skills
investment within Buckinghamshire. The project aligned closely with
the Growth Plan’s focus on innovation, business growth and
workforce development, while strengthening relationships with a
globally recognised technology and engineering company.
 
Together, these projects
demonstrated strong strategic alignment with the Growth Plan
priorities and were expected to deliver substantial economic
benefits through innovation, job creation, skills development and
wider investment attraction.
 
Full businesses cases were
presented to the Enterprise and Investment Board, Growth Board and
assessed by an external provider to provide an independent
assessment.
 
Cabinet was therefore
recommended to approve Local Growth Fund investment in the National
Autonomy & Drone Innovation Centre (NADIC) and the Robert Bosch
Centre for Innovation & Excellence, so funding agreements could
be drawn up. Early approval would enable the projects to secure
external match funding, accelerate project delivery and maximise
the economic benefits for Buckinghamshire.
 
All projects approved through
the Buckinghamshire Growth Fund, including future projects
requiring Cabinet approval, would be subject to the Council’s
established governance processes. It was proposed that funding
agreements were drafted by the Council’s Legal Services team
in collaboration with the Investment team and signed off by the
Service Director for Economy, Investment and Regeneration, in
consultation with the Leader, ensuring that all funding
arrangements were robust, compliant, and appropriately governed.
All decisions regarding the award of any future funding will be
referred back to Cabinet, with authority to sign the relevant
agreements delegated to the Service Director for Economy,
Investment & Regeneration, in consultation with the Leader,
within the parameters approved by Cabinet in those
reports.
 
RESOLVED

1)     
That the recommendations made by the Enterprise
& Investment Board and Buckinghamshire Growth Board for
investment into the time-critical investment projects be endorsed:
-
a)     
The National Autonomy & Drone Innovation
Centre (NADIC) at Westcott - £2.25m
b)    
The Robert Bosch Centre for Innovation and
Excellence at Denham - £2m

2)     
Authority be delegated to the Service Director
for Economy, Investment & Regeneration, in consultation with
the Leader, to sign off these two funding agreements. All decisions
regarding the award of any future funding will be referred back to
Cabinet, with authority to sign the relevant agreements delegated
to the Service Director for Economy, Investment & Regeneration,
in consultation with the Leader, within the parameters approved by
Cabinet in those reports.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve investment into the National Autonomy & Drone Innovation Centre and the Robert Bosch Centre for Innovation & Excellence to support economic growth in Buckinghamshire.

purpose:
The final version of the Local Plan for
Buckinghamshire to be approved for consultation and submission to
Government for an Independent Examination
content:
The
report sought Cabinet approval to publish the Buckinghamshire Local
Plan Pre-Submission (Regulation 19) version for a six-week public
consultation, prior to submission for Examination in Public by
31st December 2026.
The
Plan set out a strategy to deliver around 91,000 homes and 270
hectares of employment land with supporting infrastructure, to
2045, based on a robust and up-to-date evidence base and extensive
stakeholder engagement since 2021. It identified a spatial strategy
focused on sustainable growth taking a brownfield first approach,
extending main settlements, with the development of new
settlements, whilst having limited development in rural areas and
protecting Green Belt and areas of greatest natural beauty. It
ensured the most valued environments remained protected and set out
the importance of delivering infrastructure to support new
development. It aimed to support the Council’s ambitions to
create thriving town centres in the county’s main towns of
Aylesbury, High Wycombe and Chesham.
Progression to Regulation 19 consultation was required to meet
statutory duties and the direction from Government, and to ensure
the Council could maintain an up-to-date, plan-led approach to
managing development in line with the National Planning Policy
Framework.
The
Regulation required that the proposed submission documents,
including the proposed submission plan be made available for
consultation. Before beginning the consultation, the Council should
be satisfied that the Local Plan was sound, and that the relevant
procedural requirements had been met. Representations would be made
on these matters. The test of soundness was defined in the NPPF
paragraph 36 as being positively prepared, justified, effective and
consistent with national policy.
The
Growth Infrastructure and Select Committee undertook a
comprehensive scrutiny of the plan on the 10 July 2026 to examine
how it met the soundness tests of being positively prepared,
justified, effective, and consistent with national policy. Feedback
from the scrutiny session was available in Annex 1 to the report.
The Committee's comments and recommendations had been addressed in
the meeting and would be published with the Cabinet
papers.
RESOLVED
 
         
i.            
that the Buckinghamshire Local Plan
Pre-Submission Plan at (Appendix 1) and supporting documents
(subject to modification in (ii)) be approved, as sound, for
publication in accordance with Regulation 19 of the Town and
Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations 2012 (as
amended) and other relevant legislation and to publish the
Buckinghamshire Local Plan Pre-Submission Plan and the supporting
documents for a period of six weeks for representations, commencing
no later than 23 July 2026.
       
ii.            
that authority be delegated to the Corporate
Director for Planning, Growth and Sustainability, in consultation
with the Cabinet Member for Planning, to make any necessary minor
modifications to the Buckinghamshire Local Plan Pre-Submission Plan

purpose:
Letting of a building and approval for
procurement and delivery of refurbishment works.
content:
The
proposed transaction would convert a long-term vacant asset into an
income-generating property, while protecting and enhancing its
investment value through refurbishment works required to meet
modern market, compliance, and environmental standards. Capital
investment enabled a letting of a council-owned asset that
supported the retention of long?term employment and delivered wider
economic benefits while producing rental income for the Council.
With activity retained within Buckinghamshire, the overall impact
was positive.  The proposal represented
good value for money for the Council, providing a proportionate and
sustainable use of capital resources aligned with its strategic
objectives.
RESOLVED
1)     
That the Service Director for Corporate Property
and Assets in consultation with the Cabinet Member for Resources be
authorised to:

a.     
approve a letting of the whole of
3 Globeside, Marlow, including the
conclusion of Heads of Terms with a prospective tenant (draft terms
in Confidential Appendix 2) or an alternative tenant on
substantially similar terms, and the execution of an Agreement for
Lease and subsequent long term lease in
accordance with the agreed terms and provisional costings set out
in Confidential Appendix 3.

b.     
authorise the procurement and delivery of
refurbishment works, including the appointment of construction
consultants and entry into all necessary construction contracts to
refurbish 3 Globeside in line with
the approved specification as set out in Confidential Appendix 3,
5, 7 and 8.
2)     
That the addition and release of a project budget
to the capital programme for landlord’s capital investment
costs for the refurbishment, funded from earmarked capital
reserves, details of which are provided in Confidential Appendix 4,
be approved.

purpose:
To adopt the Tree Management Strategy
2026-2029, which addresses risk management for trees on
Council-owned land and sets out a number
of tree management policies.
content:
To adopt the Tree Management Strategy
2026-2029, which addresses risk management for trees on
Council-owned land and sets out a number
of tree management policies.

Tree Management across the
Council had up until now been applied at a service level and had
reflected the different approaches of individual services, and
legacy councils, with the risk of a disjointed approach overall.
Effective tree management delivered significant environmental,
social and economic benefits, however, realising these benefits
depended on consistency, sustained and focused investment, and an
understanding that responsible stewardship carried associated
costs.
 
This Tree Management Strategy
(TMS) had been developed to address these issues and set out the
Council’s legal obligations, policy statements, clarity on
roles and responsibilities, and management proposals. The Strategy
would be supported by an Action Plan, which outlined how the
Strategy would be implemented and the costs involved. Overall, the
Council was currently spending approximately £1.26 million
per annum on tree management. Expenditure varies across services
and would be reviewed as part of the implementation of the Tree
Management Strategy.
 
RESOLVED that the Tree Management Strategy be
adopted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt the Tree Management Strategy 2026-2029 to address risk management for trees on Council-owned land.

purpose:
Agreement with adjacent landowner to bring
forward land in High Wycombe which is allocated in the local plan
for residential development.
content:
Abbey Barn Lane was a
council-owned land parcel of 3.99 acres/1.58 hectares that was
allocated in the Wycombe District Local Plan for residential
development. It was adjacent to several other land parcels that
were also allocated for residential development. At present the
land was clear of any development and was scrubland.
 
This report sought
authorisation for the Corporate Director for Resources in
consultation with the Cabinet Member for Resources to proceed with
a conditional sale agreement of the land at Abbey Barn Lane with
the adjacent land to bring forwards residential development of the
whole site known as Abbey Barn North (“ABN”). The
conditions would be documented in the Collaboration Agreement
ensuring that the disposal meets the requirements of the
Council.
 
The objective was to pass the
risk of cost and planning onto the adjacent landowner who would
build on the development brief (attached at Appendix 3 –
Development Brief) to create one for ABN which could then be
jointly marketed for disposal and residential
development.
 
The primary financial objective
was to contribute to the capital budget target set out in the
Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP), while also satisfying the
Section 123 requirement to achieve best value in the disposal of
public assets.
 
RESOLVED that authority be delegated to the Corporate Director
for Resources in consultation with the Cabinet Member for Resources
to:

1)     
Conclude negotiations for and enter into the
Collaboration Agreement with the adjacent landowner at Abbey Barn
Lane (broadly in accordance with the draft heads of terms attached
at Confidential Appendix 1) and to take all consequential steps
necessary to enable the site to be disposed of following completion
of a planning and marketing process.

2)     
Appoint an agent to report on the best
consideration reasonably obtainable in accordance with Section 123
of the Local Government Act 1972 supporting the decision to dispose
of the site taken here.

3)     
Produce a further report to Cabinet following the
conclusion of planning and the marketing exercise, setting out the
recommended bidder and final disposal value.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to delegate authority for the conditional sale of council-owned land for residential development in Abbey Barn Lane.

purpose:
Seeking approval of the Local Transport Plan 5
and supporting Freight and Logistics Strategy for adoption
following public consultation and subsequent amendments
content:
This report sought Cabinet
approval for the LTP5 (appendix 1) and supporting Freight and
Logistics Strategy (appendix 2) to proceed to Council for adoption
as Council policy. Other supporting documents would be published
alongside LTP5 to provide technical information (appendices 4 -
7).
 
LTP5 and the supporting
documents were subject to public consultation between 16th February
and 30th March. 347 total responses were received to the public
consultation (288 survey, 59 Youth Summit). Overall, there was
strong support for the proposed policy approach. There had been no
major changes to the draft documents, but a number of minor changes
had been made to reflect the feedback received. The main changes
were addition of an accessibility theme, accessibility policy and
integrated ticketing policy. Wording had also been added throughout
the document to clarify the role of LTP5 and the delivery
processes. Key changes were summarised in appendix 3 and all
changes in appendix 9.
 
LTP5 had a similar policy
direction to LTP4 and builds on the policy approach. However, LTP5
included a greater focus on travel choice and supporting factors.
It therefore introduced new policies such as those on education and
promotion, personal safety and place shaping. LTP5 also reflected
the latest corporate priorities, best practice, policy concepts and
government requirements. Key new government requirements included
carbon analysis and inclusion of an integrated ticketing
policy.
 
The key message was that LTP5
sought to make it easier, safer and more accessible for residents
and businesses to travel while improving travel choices across the
county.
 
RESOLVED

1)     
that the consultation results and subsequent
amendments made to the draft Local Transport Plan 5 (LTP5) and
Freight and Logistics Strategy be noted.

2)     
that the draft LTP5 and Freight and Logistics
Strategy be approved to proceed to Council for
adoption.

3)     
that the approval of any minor amendments to LTP5
be delegated to the Corporate Director of Planning, Growth and
Sustainability, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for
Transport.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Local Transport Plan 5 (LTP5) and supporting Freight and Logistics Strategy to proceed to Council for adoption.

purpose:
Adoption of revised appraisal including
amended boundaries and management plan
content:
The Conservation Area for
Aylesbury had been reviewed to ensure it was up to date, fit for
purpose and to inform place-making and regeneration. Conservation
Area appraisals for key towns formed an important part of the
evidence base for the emerging Local Plan. They helped to highlight
the special character of these settlements and could help to manage
change and growth in an appropriate way.
 
A six-week public consultation
on the draft appraisal concluded on 29th October 2025. The public
consultation resulted in some changes to areas proposed for
inclusion and exclusion. These changes had been taken into account
in the final document, which was being brought forward for
adoption.
 
RESOLVED that

1)     
the amended Conservation Area boundary (Section 5
of this report and Appendix 1) be adopted.

2)     
the updated Appraisal and Management Plan
(Appendix 1) be adopted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt an amended Conservation Area boundary and an updated Appraisal and Management Plan for Aylesbury.

purpose:
Report relating to the local authority’s
submission of its SEND Reform Plan to the Department for Education
(DfE).
content:
The government published the
Schools White Paper earlier this year, setting out an ambitious
plan to create an education system where every child and young
person could achieve and thrive. This was published on Monday 23
February and included significant reform to the wider education
system and SEND.
 
On Monday 9 March, the DFE then
commissioned each Local Area Partnership to develop and submit a
Local SEND Reform Plan by 19 June 2026. The expectation being that
these documents be used to clearly set out how the Council would
improve and further strengthen its system, tilting provision
towards stronger inclusive practice and early intervention and
ensuring that the conditions underpinning effective long term outcomes were in place. 
 
Buckinghamshire’s Local
SEND Reform Plan had been developed at pace through extensive
partnership working, quality assured by DfE advisers throughout
May, and finalised and submitted by the 19 June
deadline.
 
RESOLVED that the submission of the Local SEND Reform Plan to
the DfE and the dependency on Secretary of State approval of same
to secure the High Needs Stability Grant be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to submit the Local SEND Reform Plan to the DfE for approval.

content:
The performance report provided

purpose:
To set out the Revenue outturn position for
25/26 and make any required adjustments
content:
To set out the Revenue outturn position for
25/26 and make any required adjustments

This report set out the Revenue
and Capital provisional outturn position for Buckinghamshire
Council for the financial year 2025/26. The overall position was a
surplus of £4.4m in the revenue budgets. This was a
significant success, given the financial challenges experienced by
the Council during the year and reflected an unusually high number
of positive one-off financial items alongside the strong actions
that had been successfully implemented across Cabinet Portfolios to
control expenditure.
 
The position reflected the
prudence the Council had shown in managing its budgets,
particularly in Adult Social Care, Home to School Transport and
Temporary Accommodation. In addition, early delivery of savings and
the Council’s track record of effective service reviews had
helped deliver a positive position in relation to
staffing.However, with the growth in demand
continuing to be seen, the volatility in the world, and closer to
home, along with inflation pressures impacting the economy, next
year would be even more challenging. The 2027/28 Medium Term
Financial Plan process would review where the Council had been
successful in delivering an underspend in 2025/26 for any ongoing
benefit.
 

RESOLVED that
1)     
the report and the success in achieving a
£4.4m revenue surplus in 2025/26 be noted.
2)     
the transfers to reserves as set out in paragraph
2.6 of the Cabinet report be approved.
3)     
the overall capital outturn position of
£155.8m of investment in the Council’s priorities be
noted.
4)     
the carry-forward of capital budgets as detailed
in section 4 of the Cabinet report be approved.
5)     
authority be delegated to the S151 Officer in
consultation with the Leader to make any amendments required to
finalise the outturn position.
6)     
the confidential appendix relating to the Energy
from Waste legal case which is exempt under the Local Government
Act 1972, Schedule 12A, Paragraph 3 (financial affairs) be
noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the success of achieving a £4.4m revenue surplus in 2025/26 and approve necessary adjustments to the outturn position.

purpose:
To note the revised Skills and Employment
Strategy.
content:
To note the revised Skills and Employment
Strategy.

The revised Buckinghamshire
Skills and Employment Strategy set out a place-based approach to
skills and employment across the county. Developed collaboratively
by the Skills Strategy Board with Buckinghamshire employers, Sector
Leads, Education providers, BBF, DWP and the Council, it reflected
a shared commitment to an ambitious, joined-up and inclusive skills
and employment system.
 
It was aligned with the
Buckinghamshire Economic Growth Plan, Local Skills and Improvement
Plan (LSIP); Buckinghamshire Works and national policy, ensuring
that skills investment responded directly to local economic need
and community priorities.
 
The Strategy provided a
coherent framework to inform commissioning, investment and delivery
decisions across skills and employment, ensuring activity was
evidence led, employer informed and aligned with
Buckinghamshire’s economic growth priorities.  The Strategy had been approved by the Growth
Board.
 
RESOLVED that the revised Buckinghamshire Skills and Employment
Strategy, which sets out a place-based strategic framework for
skills and employment and which aligns with and supports the
delivery of the Buckinghamshire Growth Plan, be endorsed.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to endorse the revised Buckinghamshire Skills and Employment Strategy.

purpose:
To report to Cabinet on the work undertaken by
the Committee (which is an Executive Sub-Committee of Cabinet)
during 2025/26.
content:
The
role of the Shareholder and Trust Committee was to ensure that the
Council’s companies, limited liability partnerships and
trusts acted in the interests of the Council as shareholder and in
the case of trusts, sole trustee, and that best practice was being
adhered to in delivering statutory arrangements. In doing so, the
Committee contributed to the proper governance of the
Council’s subsidiaries and trusts. This added level of
governance continued to be vitally important in the context of the
financial challenges many local authorities had faced over recent
years with local authority companies and trusts. Understanding the
risks and performance associated with wholly or jointly owned
companies and trusts was a key task of the Committee.
Producing an annual report to reflect the work and outcomes
achieved by the Committee throughout 2025-26 was considered good
practice.
It
was noted that Members of the Shareholder and Trust Committee were
not directors, and did not have any direct involvement, in any of
the subsidiary bodies.
RESOLVED
that the Buckinghamshire Shareholder & Trust Committee Annual
Report which details the work undertaken during 2025/26 be
noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the Buckinghamshire Shareholder & Trust Committee Annual Report for 2025/26.

purpose:
To endorse the Best Start Plan and agree the
approach to designating Best Start Family Hubs
content:
Cabinet received a report which set out Buckinghamshire
Council’s proposals to deliver the Government’s Best
Start in Life programme through the development of an enhanced
Family Hub model, focused on improving outcomes for children in
their earliest years and reducing inequalities in child
development. The approach recognised that most families were
resilient and parent their children without needing additional
support from the Council, while ensuring timely and targeted
support for those families who did need it.
The
Best Start in Life programme required local authorities to
strengthen early years and family services to support national
ambitions for children’s development, measured through the
Good Level of Development (GLD) at the end of the reception year.
Buckinghamshire had been set an ambitious statutory target of 80%
of children achieving a GLD by 2027/28, alongside a significant
improvement for children eligible for free school meals. Achieving
this required early, preventative support for families facing
greater challenge, rather than universal intervention.
Building on an established network of family centres and a
strong system of partnership working, the Council proposed to
designate a further two Best Start Family Hubs in areas of higher
need and inequality: High Wycombe and Burnham. These hubs would sit
within the wider Family Hub Network, providing enhanced,
place?based support during pregnancy and the first five years of
life for families who needed it most, while maintaining a universal
family centre offer which remained open and accessible to all
communities across the county.
Elmhurst Family Centre in Aylesbury had been designated as
Buckinghamshire’s first Best Start Family Hub from April
2026, acting as an early pathfinder for the programme. Learning
from Elmhurst would inform the phased development of Best Start
Family Hubs in High Wycombe and Burnham, ensuring a consistent
approach which supported family resilience, intervened early where
required, and allowed flexibility to respond to local
needs.
In
High Wycombe, GLD performance data demonstrated a clear case for
establishing a Best Start Family Hub to strengthen early support
for families experiencing disadvantage. Work was underway to assess
which existing family centre site would be most suitable for
expansion and co?location, with a recommendation that Cabinet
confirmed High Wycombe as a priority location and delegated the
final site decision to the Cabinet Member for Education and
Children’s Services. Outreach and blended delivery would
ensure that support reached families most in need, regardless of
the physical hub location.
Burnham had been identified as a priority location due to
particularly low GLD outcomes for children from disadvantaged
backgrounds, alongside clear constraints within the existing family
centre building. The Cabinet report proposed retaining and
repurposing the former Day Opportunities Centre in Burnham, rather
than proceeding with disposal of the site, to enable relocation and
expansion of family services. This would provide a welcoming
setting where families could access early help when challenges
arose, supporting resilience and preventing escalation, with the
aim of establishing the hub by January 2027.
The
recommendations in the Cabinet report sought Cabinet agreement to
the overall Best Start in Life approach, the designation of new
Best Start Family Hub locations, and the strategic use of Council
assets to support delivery. Taken together, these proposals would
strengthen early intervention while recognising family resilience,
ensuring that support would be available when needed and targeted
appropriately. This would improve long?term outcomes for children
and families and support the Council’s wider ambition to
ensure every child in Buckinghamshire had the best possible start
in life.
RESOLVED
that

a)     
the Best Start in Life Programme be
endorsed.

b)    
following the designation of Elmhurst in
Aylesbury, a further two locations for Best Start Family Hubs
(BSFH) - High Wycombe and Burnham - be agreed.

c)     
authority be delegated to the Cabinet Member for
Education and Children’s Services to decide on the site
location of the High Wycombe BSFH.

d)    
it be agreed to retain the building of the former
Adult Day Opportunities centre in Burnham and repurpose, with
capital investment, as a BSFH from January 2027 at the earliest
(replacing the existing Family Centre in Burnham).

e)     
it be agreed to fund a £678,000 Capital
Budget to deliver the Best Start Family Hubs, funded from Best
Start Grant £338k and Corporate Capital funding £340k
from the capital programme contingency. This will be subject to
Capital Gateway approval once works costs are
confirmed.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to endorse the Best Start in Life Programme and designate new locations for Family Hubs to improve outcomes for children in Buckinghamshire.

purpose:
To present the outcome and recommendations
following a quantitative and qualitative options appraisal of the
current and potential future operational arrangements for the Waste
Collections and Street Scene Services.
content:
Waste Collection and Street Scene Services
were currently delivered through an in-house arrangement in the
north of the county and through an outsourced contract (currently
with Veolia until 2030) in the south of the county. Waste
Collection and Street Scene Services were a key priority for the
Council, residents and businesses, with an average of 627,000
collections made per week in Buckinghamshire.
 
The Cabinet report proposed that the Council
implemented a single, outsourced model for the delivery of Waste
Collections and Street Scene Services from October 2029, replacing
the current ‘mixed economy’ of service provision
(delivered in-house in the North of the county, and outsourced in
the South). The recommendation followed an assessment of a range of
potential delivery options against qualitative and quantitative
criteria, with the single outsourced option scoring highest in both
the elements of the appraisal and also following sensitivity
analysis. Aligning North and South operations under a single,
county wide, high quality contracted model was expected to enhance
value for money for the Council and provide year on year savings.
Given the scale of the new contract, the opportunity
Buckinghamshire presented, and the buoyancy and maturity of the
outsourced market, it was anticipated that the procurement would
attract significant market interest / competition from major
suppliers and promote a competitive procurement process.
 
The proposal was to align current services
into a single outsourced contract, ensuring residents experience a
consistent service with no reduction in current standards. Equality
considerations would be included in the contract specification to
safeguard inclusion, and the EqIA
(Appendix 6) would be kept under review and updated as / when
required. The proposal would ensure continued, high-standard waste
and street scene services for everyone living, working, studying,
or visiting Buckinghamshire.

 
RESOLVED that

1.     
a single outsourced model for Waste Collection
and Street Scene services in Buckinghamshire, with a staggered
start (October 2029 for Northern services and September 2030 for
Southern services) be implemented.

2.     
the procurement process for a single
(county-wide) contract be started from April 2026, with an expected
service commencement date of October 2029.

3.     
authority be delegated to the
Service Director for Neighbourhood Services, in consultation with
the Leader of the Council and the Cabinet Member for Environment,
Climate Change and Waste, to lead a compliant procurement process,
including adherence to procurement regulation, Procurement Act
2023.

4.     
following the procurement process, Cabinet to
approve the award of the contract to provide Waste Collection and
Street Scene services in Buckinghamshire.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to implement a single outsourced model for Waste Collection and Street Scene services in Buckinghamshire, aiming to enhance value for money and provide year on year savings.

purpose:
This report sets out proposals for
funding allocations from the new Crisis and Resilience
Fund to support Buckinghamshire residents between
April 2026 and March 2027 in line with government
guidance.
content:
The Government had launched a
new Crisis and Resilience Fund (CRF) to support people who
experience a financial shock and to support financial resilience.
This fund replaced the Household Support Fund (HSF) and the
Discretionary Housing Payment (DHP). The Government had reduced
funding to Buckinghamshire Council for assisting individuals facing
financial hardship. Over the past two years, total grant support
had been reduced by more than £600,000.
 
The new Government guidance set
out detailed requirements that the Council must follow to
administer the grant, including a significant change in approach
from the previous Household Support Fund. The Government was
seeking to shift funding away from crisis support and towards
prevention and financial resilience. The new objectives of the fund
were to provide a safety net for those on low incomes who encounter
a financial shock and to invest in building local financial
resilience.
 
The new government grant
conditions affected families receiving free school meal vouchers
during holidays. Previously, eligible families automatically
received vouchers, but this was no longer compatible with grant
conditions. Now, local authorities must target support to
households in financial crisis and who were experiencing sudden
financial shock, based on evidence of individual need, rather than
giving vouchers to all recipients of free school meals who might
not require that support on a regular basis.
 
The Council was committed to
continuing to support its residents and communities in financial
hardship. The Council was aware how vital financial support was for
our residents and how much they valued the vital crisis support
provided. The Council would do this through supporting families to
access the Holiday Activities and Food (HAF) programme, which
included providing hot meals for children during the school
holidays; through supporting residents to access crisis payments
and helping residents to access money and debt advice through the
Council’s commissioned service with Citizens
Advice.
 
The Council also planned to
introduce a new financial resilience community fund of
£800,000 in the first year to help communities manage the
cost of living. This fund aimed to empower voluntary and community
groups to develop innovative ways to support financial stability
locally. The Council would collaborate with Heart of Bucks to
ensure strong partnerships and effective community
involvement.
 
RESOLVED that

1)     
the arrangements for deploying the new Crisis and
Resilience Fund allocation for 2026/27 be approved.

2)     
the reduction in government funding and new
Government guidance on grant expenditure to support those in
financial crisis and to support financial resilience be
noted.

3)     
the new Crisis and Resilience Fund policy as set
out in Appendix 1 be agreed.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the new Crisis and Resilience Fund allocation to support individuals facing financial hardship and promote financial resilience.

purpose:
This paper outlines implementation of the
current Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy and action plan,
and recommends a strategy refresh in 2027
content:
The governments new
homelessness strategy, A National Plan to End Homelessness, was
published in December 2025. The Strategy urged all councils to
critically evaluate their homelessness strategies and transition
from a reactive, crisis-driven approach to one focused on
prevention, while undertaking a detailed review to prepare for
future changes. The December announcement reiterated the needed
alignment to the Act and a five year time period for strategies. A
revised strategy would be developed for adoption in April 2027.
This strategy would ensure alignment with the Homelessness Act
2002, the Government’s new strategy (announced December 2025)
and further strengthen partnership working.
 
The Cabinet Member reported
that the Council was maintaining momentum by:-
 

·        
improving homelessness
prevention 

·        
reducing temporary accommodation
demand 

·        
controlling costs
and strengthening rough sleeping pathways. 
 
Key progress
included:-
 

Improvement of Prevention activity, with more
households successfully avoiding homelessness. Over 600 households would have been prevented from
homelessness by the end of this year.


Temporary accommodation demand was down compared
with the same time last year. 


Temporary accommodation
costs remained significantly lower than historic
nightly?paid models. This had saved
£1.5 million a year.


Affordable housing
delivery remained strong, helping reduce long?term
pressure. 3000 homes had been delivered
over the last six years (506 a year). A Bucks Let Scheme was also
being introduced to help move people into permanent
homes.
Rough sleeping pathways had been strengthened
through targeted outreach and specialist support such as the use of
the Making Every Adult Matter Team. 

 
Another specific example of improvements and progress, in
partnership with a local provider, the Council was poised
to deliver 42 new supported temporary accommodation units
in Aylesbury later this month. These would support people
with more complex needs, helping them build independence
and move on more quickly into settled
housing. 
 
Cabinet noted the progress
under the current Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy. As the
Government had published a new National Plan to End
Homelessness with a prevention?first approach, extending the
current strategy kept the Council compliant and avoided unnecessary
rewrites while enabling a full evidence?based assessment in
2026. The current strategy remained fit for
purpose. This was a timeline alignment with no new financial
implications and remained consistent with the Medium?Term
Financial Plan. 
The next steps
were:-
 

Comprehensive assessment in 2026 to inform the
2027–2032 strategy. 


Continued delivery through the existing action
plan. 


Progress reporting to Select Committee in Autumn
2026. 


September Cabinet to receive draft 2027 Strategy
ahead of full consultation for 6 weeks, ahead of formal
consideration in March 2027. 

 
This approach allowed the Council to continue delivering
what was working now while building a stronger, evidence?led,
prevention?first strategy for the future. 
 
RESOLVED that
 
1.
the significant work undertaken to date to implement the
Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy (2022-25) be acknowledged
and that the end date of the existing strategy be extended to 2027
to align with Government guidance; and
 
2. a
new Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy be developed with a
five year time horizon with a proposed adoption of April
2027.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to extend the existing Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy to align with the government's new National Plan to End Homelessness, with a new strategy to be developed for adoption in April 2027.

purpose:
A report to recommend the approach for the
future redevelopment of Easton Street Multistorey Car Park
site.
content:
The Council’s Easton
Street Multistorey Car Park (ESMCP) was dated, suffered from
structural, health and safety and anti-social behaviour issues. It
currently operated at a financial net loss and would require
substantial capital investment to remain viable. With sufficient
alternative parking provision in the surrounding area, the site was
now recommended as surplus for parking purposes.
 
Following the Council’s
decision to close parking decks 6 to 12 and decommission the lifts
at ESMCP, a further decision was now required to permanently close
the facility by March 2026 and proceed with demolition. This would
enable the council to dispose of the asset and secure value for
money. In line with the commercial advice, demolition was necessary
to realise a capital receipt from the site. Furthermore, this
approach removed any ongoing financial liability associated with
operational and security costs. A subsequent report would be
brought forward following further analysis to determine the most
appropriate way forward to realise a capital receipt and unlock
regeneration.
 
Crucially, this location was
identified as a strategic site with the Council’s High
Wycombe Regeneration Strategy and formed a cornerstone of the
Easton Quarter Vision. This presented a unique opportunity to
unlock transformational regeneration, creating a vibrant new
destination that aligned with the council's long term regeneration
ambitions for High Wycombe.
 
The Cabinet
Member reported that two representations had been received which
have been considered by Cabinet Members. One from Trinity United
Reformed Church and the other from the Union Baptist
Church.
 
He also reported
that full restoration of the car park would cost £3 million
and was currently operating at a loss of £253,000 annually.
The current occupancy of the remaining six floors was 63.9% with a
10% adjustment to account for Council staff who held permits.
Following closure of the car park residents would be redirected to
nearby facilities such as the Swan Car Park (at 55% capacity - 323
spaces in total) or Railway Place (at 60% capacity – 182
spaces in total). Therefore, there was sufficient capacity for
displaced demand. There would be proactive engagement and
communications to ensure a smooth transition to nearby
facilities.
 
RESOLVED that
 
1. the permanent closure of Easton Street
Multistorey Car Park from March 2026 be approved including the
demolition of Easton Street Multistorey Car Park
 
2. the funding of the demolition costs be
approved, estimated at £1.750m to be met from the future
disposal proceeds of the site and for this to be added to the
Capital Programme.
 
3. authority be delegated to the Service
Director for Highways & Technical Services and Service Director
for Corporate Property & Assets in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Parking Services & Cabinet Member for
Resources for the following:
 
a. To procure and undertake all relevant
workstreams that facilitate the advancement of the demolition
works
 
b. To undertake a procurement exercise for a
demolition contractor and to then subsequently enter a demolition
contract to advance the demolition works with the preferred
contractor and to enter into any necessary agreements with
adjoining landowners to facilitate the demolition works of Easton
Street Multistorey Car Park.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to permanently close and demolish the Easton Street Multistorey Car Park to unlock regeneration opportunities in High Wycombe.

purpose:
Action Plan to deliver LGA Peer Challenge
Recommendations
content:
In autumn 2025, Buckinghamshire
Council took part in a Corporate Peer Challenge (CPC). Across four
days, from 30 September to 3 October 2025, a team of highly
experienced senior local government councillor and officer peers
from other local authorities visited Buckinghamshire Council to
meet with Members, officers, and partners. This was the first CPC
as Buckinghamshire Council and the review had provided both a
powerful endorsement of the work already undertaken, with peers
calling Buckinghamshire “one of the best run councils the
peer reviewers had ever visited", and a useful roadmap for further
improvements in the future.
 
The next step was now to
produce and publish a formal action plan, setting out how it would
respond to the recommendations made by the peer team. The Council
was required to publish this plan within five months of the review
taking place. The action plan translated the peer challenge
findings into a focused programme of improvement activity,
identifying key actions, responsibilities and timescales. In line
with LGA expectations, the Corporate Peer Challenge action plan
must be published. In the summer of 2026, a number of the peer team
would return to Buckinghamshire and review the progress of the
action plan, and the changes which have been made as a
result.
 
The Leader reported that there
were 30 actions covering strategic priorities and finance,
governance, employee culture and engagement, empowering communities
and regeneration and housing. 
 
RESOLVED that the CPC action plan in response to the LGA
Corporate Peer Challenge recommendations be agreed.
topline: The Buckinghamshire Council has decided to produce and publish a formal action plan in response to a Corporate Peer Challenge for further improvements.

purpose:
For Cabinet to note the update on the Ofsted

children in care, and care leavers).
content:
For Cabinet to note the update on the Ofsted
Recommendations Improvement Plan (following the ILACS inspection in
early 2025 in relation to children in need of help and protection,
children in care, and care leavers).

Ofsted conducted a standard
ILACS (Inspecting Local Authority Children’s Services)
inspection of Buckinghamshire Council between 27 January and 7
February 2025. The inspection focused on services for children in
need of help and protection, children in care, and care leavers.
The final report was published on 14 May 2025. An improvement plan
was developed to help address the areas requiring improvement. The
report provided an update on the areas within the plan.
 
The Cabinet Member for
Children’s and Education reported that the last inspection
was in 2021 and they identified key
areas for improvement which included:-

·        
The impact of leaders on social work practice for
children and families

·        
The experiences and progress for children who needed
protection, for children in care and
also for care leavers
 
At this last Inspection the
Inspectors found areas of improvement and changed the rating from
‘requires improvement’ to ‘good’. Ofsted
found that children that came into care did so at an appropriate
time and received good care. They praised:-
·        
the ambition to improve placement
sufficiency,
·        
supplying in-county children’s
homes
·        
the progress made in recruiting more foster
carers.
·        
referrals to MASH for children at risk were
responded to in a timely manner
·        
the assessments carried out by social workers and
the good relationship they had built with the child including
reducing agency staff
·        
disabled children were looked after by social
workers who understood their needs
·        
working with other agencies to reduce the risk of
exploitation
·        
good school attendance
 
Areas where Ofsted identified
further improvements were required was support for care leavers
with a call for more consistency. The improvement plan covered the
following areas:-
 
·        
The quality and robustness of management oversight
to promote consistently effective social work (National Framework
enabler two).
·        
The quality and effectiveness of the service to
children who were at risk from neglect (National Framework outcome
three).
·        
The consistency and timeliness of work to engage a
child’s wider family network (National Framework outcome
two).
·        
The efficacity of transition planning for older
children in care and disabled young people leaving care (National
Framework outcome four).
·        
The quality and effectiveness of pathway plans for
care leavers (National Framework outcome four).
·        
The quality of service and support to care leavers
aged 21+ (National Framework outcome four).
·        
The engagement and participation of care-experienced
children and young people in the corporate parenting board
(National Framework enabler two).
 
The Cabinet Member thanked all
the staff who worked in this area.
 
RESOLVED that the Ofsted Recommendations Improvement Plan (see
Appendix of the report) be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the update on the Ofsted Recommendations Improvement Plan for children in need of help and protection, children in care, and care leavers.

purpose:
This paper presents findings and
recommendations following the publication of a report by the Local
Government Social Care Ombudsman (LGSCO)
content:
This paper presents findings and
recommendations following the publication of a report by the Local
Government Social Care Ombudsman (LGSCO)

The Local Government and Social
Care Ombudsman (LGSCO) had published a Public Interest Report (PIR)
following an investigation into a complaint about Buckinghamshire
Council’s arrangements for securing therapy provision set out
in two children’s Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs) in
2023/24. The Ombudsman found fault with the Council in respect of
missed speech and language therapy (SLT) and occupational therapy
(OT), delays in the EHCP review and amendment process, together
with shortcomings in complaint handling. The Ombudsman had decided
to publish the final report in the public interest because it
considered the complaint revealed wider systemic issues.
 
The report provided Cabinet
with information on the findings in the PIR. It also set out the
Council’s intended approach to publication. Whilst the
Council had already made significant changes and improvements in
the relevant services since the period referenced in the PIR, the
report also described how the Council would meet the
Ombudsman’s recommendations.
 
The Cabinet Member reported
that at this time speech and language therapy was provided for 400
children by a private contractor and in March 2024 that arrangement
ended and the NHS Healthcare Trust took over responsibility for
providing that therapy. There was additional funding to help the
transition and support provided by the Council at that time. The
two children referred to in the report received some of the support
that they were entitled too but not all.
 
In relation to child X, the
Ombudsman upheld the complaint that child X did not receive the SLT
or OT provision set out in his EHCP between September 2023 and
December 2024. The Ombudsman concluded that child X received less
than half of the SLT provision specified and almost none of the OT
provision, and that no arrangement was made to provide therapy to
make up for the shortfall during the remainder of the academic
year.
 
In relation to child Y, the
Ombudsman accepted the Council’s view that it believed child
Y no longer needed regular SLT following discharge from the therapy
service in 2022. However, child Y’s EHCP continued to include
SLT provision in Section F. The Ombudsman found fault because the
Council remained under a duty to secure the provision that remained
in the EHCP until the EHCP was amended.
 
The Ombudsman found fault with
the Council’s complaint handling, due to delays in responding
to the complaint at both stages of the Council’s complaints
process. The Ombudsman also raised a wider concern that, although
the Council acknowledged service failings, it did not seek to
remedy missed provision in line with the Ombudsman’s
published guidance on remedies.
 
The Ombudsman recommended that
the Council issue a formal apology to the complainant and make a
symbolic payment to recognise the missed provision for child X and
child Y and the distress and uncertainty caused by delays and
shortcomings in provision and process. A formal apology had been
made but the Cabinet Member apologised again at the meeting for not
providing the full support to those children in 2023/24, which was
also reiterated by the Leader.
 
Three specific improvements
were identified as follows:-
 

·      
The Council should set out a plan for how it would
tackle any shortfall in meeting the needs of children and young
people with EHCPs whose needs were not currently met by the therapy
service.

·      
The Council should develop a protocol for cases
where the therapy service was unable to deliver therapy provision
in line with a child's EHCP and set out alternatives.

·      
The Council should provide a briefing to staff who
deal with complaints about special educational needs provision,
setting out the expectation that when the Council identified a
service failing it would consider ways of remedying that in line
with published guidance on remedies. The Cabinet Member reported
that this briefing had taken place.
 
The Cabinet Member corrected a
recent media report which commented that the 400 children who had
been transitioned had not received support which was not the case;
the fault only lay with child x and y. The Ombudsman had corrected
this information on their website.
 
The Council had already made
significant changes and improvements in the relevant services since
the period referenced in the PIR. In 2024, the Council agreed and
published its strategy ‘Early Intervention and Prevention to
Better Support Children and Young People’s Therapy
Needs’, and more recently the Council and partners adopted
the local SEND and Inclusion Strategy which set out how every child
would receive the right support at the right time. These strategies
demonstrated the Council’s commitment to continued
improvement for children and young people with SEND in
Buckinghamshire, working collaboratively with key partners
including BHT. The recent SEND Local Area inspection report also
recognised that therapy services have been transformed through
investment in staffing, training and a new integrated care model
that was more accessible to children and families. Communications
had also been improved with families and the Inspector also
recognised the improvement in the quality of EHCPs and a recovery
plan was in place to cut waiting times.
 
The Chief Nurse also reported
on the improvements made since 2024. Significant work had been
undertaken to reduce the waiting times previously at 60% of
children not being seen within 18 weeks and now there were only 18
children waiting over that time period.
 
RESOLVED that the findings and recommendations made by the Local
Government and Social Care Ombudsman and the actions the Council is
taking in response to these be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to acknowledge fault in missed therapy provision for children in EHCPs and implement improvements in therapy services following findings from the Local Government Social Care Ombudsman.

purpose:
Woodlands Aylesbury – Proposed contract
with Developer
content:
The report set out the current
position regarding the negotiated condition precedent contract
between Buckinghamshire Advantage and The Developer regarding the
Woodlands development site in Aylesbury. The contract negotiations
had reached a position that both parties had agreed a finalised
version of the contract, which was now materially agreed. The
contract set out the delivery of the Woodlands site including land
assembly, infrastructure delivery and housing (and employment site)
delivery.
 
The site was allocated for
development in the Vale of Aylesbury Local Plan. Aylesbury was a
key area of growth in the UK with over 16,000 homes planned to be
delivered in the VALP and in 2017 Aylesbury obtained Garden Town
designation. A significant part of the site fell within the
Aylesbury Woodlands/Arla Enterprise Zone, which was designated by
Central Government in 2015. Woodlands was a fundamental part of a
long-term strategy to deliver an orbital traffic route around
Aylesbury, delivering the Eastern Link Road (South) (ELRS). The
ELRS would connect to the Eastern Link Road (North) that had
already been substantially delivered as part of the Kingsbrook
development and the Southern Link Road to be delivered by Hampden
Fields (Taylor Wimpey).
 
Buckinghamshire Advantage was a
100% owned subsidiary to the Council, that had been responsible for
funding the Planning Application for Woodlands and securing options
with landowners. The Shareholder and Trust Committee had reviewed
this proposal a number of times and were fully in support of the
recommendation.
 
As part of the Woodlands
outline planning permission secured in April 2022, the ELRS was to
be delivered as a single carriageway with land reserved for
widening and main junctions delivered capable of accommodating a
future dual carriageway.
 
The contract summary in the
confidential appendices set out the full list of conditions
precedent. These included reserved matters applications, land
assembly and LGF & HIF funding agreement. The Council was
currently in negotiation with Homes England to secure an extension
to the HIF funding agreement to allow for any potential delays in
the delivery of the Eastern Link Road and would be in a stronger
position to do this when the contract was signed.
 
The Leader commented that the
proposal provided a significant opportunity to enhance local
quality of life and economic resilience. Specifically
it:-
 

·        
Created an opportunity site capable of bringing
forward high?quality commercial and residential floorspace,
supporting job creation and offering new housing options for local
people.

·        
Secured sustainable transport measures on the
approaches to Aylesbury, helping to encourage greener travel
choices.

·        
Contributed to improvements in local air quality by
providing relief to town centre Air Quality Management Areas,
thereby supporting public health and wellbeing.
 
RESOLVED
 
1.That Buckinghamshire Advantage enter the Condition Precedent
Contract between Buckinghamshire Advantage and the developer. This
has been finalised by the parties pursuant to the Decision by
Cabinet in March last year.
 
2. To
complete the contract once condition precedents are satisfied,
funding agreement has been secured (or waived by agreement of the
parties (where possible)
 
3.
That the Council release £3.4m of funding for future
management of the project from Homes England. This funding will
only be used when Housing Infrastructure Funding has been agreed
with Homes England to cover these costs, or that an alternative
funding source has been identified. This will include management,
legal, marketing & CPO arrangements.
 
4.
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Special
Projects in consultation with the Cabinet Member for Resources and
S151 Officer to approve capped further loans to Buckinghamshire
Advantage to facilitate the delivery of the obligations under the
Condition Precedent contract.
 
Cabinet to Note;
 
The
Condition Precedent Contract includes pre-emption/Options for the
Council, a Special Purpose Vehicle or Buckinghamshire Advantage to
bring forward the employment land and the sports facilities on the
Woodlands site all of which would be the subject of (a) further
report(s) to Cabinet
 
Land
assembly contracts with various landowners will take place to meet
the requirements of the conditions precedent contract.
 
Buckinghamshire Council seek to progress accelerated delivery of
Woodlands such as Phase 1B of the ELR, Archaeological and
Ecological work.
 
As
per previous delegations secured in the March 2025 Cabinet report.
There is authorisation to complete signing of the conditions
precedent contract between Buckinghamshire Advantage and the
developer.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to finalize a contract for the Woodlands development site in Aylesbury, paving the way for significant economic and infrastructure improvements.

purpose:
Update to the Local Development Scheme,
setting out the Local Plan programme to adoption.
content:
The Local Development Scheme
(LDS) set out the timetable for the production of Local Development
Documents (LDDs) which include the Local Plan and associated
documents. Councils were required to produce the LDS in accordance
with the Planning and Compulsory Purchase Act 2004 (as amended).
Where appropriate it should also include details of other documents
that will form part of the development plan, for example
neighbourhood plans.
 
The LDS and any amendments made
to it must be made publicly available and should be published on
the Council’s website and kept up-to-date. The LDS had been
updated to reflect the current position of the Local Plan and other
development plans and to respond to Matthew Pennycook’s
(Minister of State for Housing and Planning) letter in February
2026 requiring key milestones to be met by specific dates (Appendix
1). This was to ensure the Local Plan remained on track for
submitting the Local Plan for Examination by 31st December
2026.
 
The Leader commented that he
had written to the Minister stating that the Council was meeting
the timetable that had been set. This was undertaken after the
Government had changed the housing target for Buckinghamshire with
a 43% increase to 5,500 homes. The Council had met all the
milestones set out in March 2025. The current engagement on site
selection remained open for a few days. Since becoming a unitary
authority in 2025, £3.2m had been spent on the Local Plan.
£1.8m remained in the Local Plan reserve as of the end of the
financial year for 2025/26.
 
The Cabinet Member confirmed
the absolute commitment of the Council to deliver a robust Local
Plan on time. The Minister MP Matthew Pennycook requested that the
LDS be revised and published on the Council’s website by 11th
March 2026. The Government had been explicit that the Council must
publish. Regulation 19 consultation would still commence by no
later than 23 July 2026 following consideration at Cabinet on 22
July. This would be the final version of the Plan before it was
submitted for examination. The Council was firmly on track to meet
these milestones.
 
The Corporate Director also
commented that the Government were revoking the legal Duty to
Co-operate for the plan making process. This was a legal test
required by all neighbouring authorities, but the Government felt
that this was slowing the process down. However, the National
Planning Policy Framework still expected there to be effective
engagement in relation to housing and employment
numbers.
 
RESOLVED that the updated Local Development Scheme is to have
effect from 11th March 2026 and that authority be delegated to the
Corporate Director for Planning, Growth and Sustainability in
consultation with Cabinet Member for Planning to approve any
necessary minor amendments to the Local Development
Scheme.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the updated Local Development Scheme to meet key milestones for the Local Plan submission by the end of 2026.

purpose: Quarterly report
content:
This report set out the
forecast Revenue and Capital outturn position for Buckinghamshire
Council for the financial year 2025/26 as at Quarter 3. Overall,
the forecast revenue outturn was a balanced position. The Council
continued to experience significant financial pressures from
increases in demand and complexity of need in the key services of
Children’s Social Care, Temporary Accommodation and High
Needs budgets within the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).
 
The forecast revenue outturn
position at Quarter 3 within Portfolios was an adverse variance of
£0.8m (0.2% of Portfolio budgets), compared with £2.1m
adverse reported at Q2. The pressures in the forecast were in
Children’s Social Care Provider Services £6.0m and
Temporary Accommodation £0.8m, offset by £3.0m in
Planning from additional planning income and an underspend of
£1.6m in Transport. A balanced position overall was due to a
favourable variance in Corporate and Funding budgets.
 
The Dedicated Schools Grant
budget had been set with a deficit of £22.9m. Currently the
forecast position was slightly over budget (£0.18m).
£3m was being transferred to reserves to fund investment to
improve waiting times in processing of EHCPs. The balance on the
DSG deficit reserve at the beginning of the year was £24.5m
with a forecast closing balance of £47.58m.
 
The forecast position on
capital budgets was £160.7m, with £13.2m (7.6%)
rephasing against the budget of £173.8m. This was ahead of
the Cabinet’s target of 10% slippage, and ahead of the
position in the previous year, with progress made in key projects
during Q3. The budget included an approved savings programme of
£115.6m over 3 years, with £76.9m to be delivered in
2025/26. Delivery of savings for 2025/26 was currently forecast at
0.4% above target with a total £0.3m of savings above budget.
Actions would continue to be required to closely manage the in-year
financial position.
 
RESOLVED that the report be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations on the forecast Revenue and Capital outturn position for Buckinghamshire Council for the financial year 2025/26.
