purpose:
For Cabinet to recommend the final budget to
Council
content:
Cabinet received the report on
the Medium-Term Financial Plan 2026/27 to 2028/29 and Capital
Programme 2026/27 to 2029/30. The draft budget had already been
discussed at the Cabinet Meeting on 8 January 2026. The budget was
then discussed at Budget Scrutiny and there were no recommendations
that changed the budget figures. The report included information on
the Council Tax Reduction Scheme.
 
The Leader referred again to
the Fair Funding Review which meant a reduction in the budget of
£44.5 million. The proposal was to increase Council Tax by
4.99%. Nationally £6 billion had been put into a recovery
grant for the next three years designed to address the funding gap
which included £440 million uplift for urban and metropolitan
areas.
 
Members noted that the Council
had been anticipating this reform and had made £23.6 million
savings towards this impact. A balanced budget was still proposed
over the three-year period with all these challenges whilst
providing good quality services such as regular bin collections,
planning enforcement and spending on roads and transport
(£220 million investment of which £120 million would be
spent on roads). There was also a £600 million capital
programme which would be used for the benefit of residents on areas
such as children’s homes which should help reduce the
pressure on the revenue budget.
 
The Leader reported on an
update for the Final Local Government Settlement. There was no
change to the Funding Formula so there was still a reduction of
£44.5 million which would be sent to Councils in other areas
of the Country under the Fair Funding Review. Over a £1
million was received for ringfenced grants for homelessness and
rough sleeping and to tackle domestic abuse. There had been a
change to the Dedicated Schools Grant. Many Councils had a
statutory override in place as there was insufficient funding for
Special Educational Needs. There was a deficit in this area in the
Country of £14 billion and the Government was going to
transfer this cost to central government in 2028. There had been a
recent announcement that the Government would cover this deficit up
until 2028 through grants of up to 90%. For the 10% which was
unfunded for Buckinghamshire in the first year it would cost
£4.7 million and over the three years £13.7 million.
Adjustments would need to be made therefore at the year end to
balance the budget.
 
The Section 151 Officer
reported that the grant funding had conditions attached which
included the submission of a SEND plan which would be produced
collaboratively with schools, post-16 and early years settings. The
Council would not receive the funding until this had been approved
by DfE in Autumn 2026.
 
The Section 151 Officer also
reported that there were no recommended changes to the budget as a
result of the Council Tax Reduction Scheme consultation. The
Cabinet Member reminded Members that there was a proposal to amend
the CTRS which had been consulted upon to start from 1 April. The
proposals should reduce volatility for households, simplify
assessments, remove reliance on the DWP and reduce processing
times. A consultation ran from 17 December to 2 February and 518
responses were received. The vast majority of comments recognise
the need for modernisation of the scheme. 18 responses argued for
the retention of the scheme. There were concerns that the scheme
would include the loss of the 25% single person discount and
communications reassured residents that this was not the case and
there was no impact. The proposals would therefore be considered at
Full Council.
 
RESOLVED to RECOMMEND that Full Council
 

·        
approve the Medium-Term Financial Plan
2026/276 to 2028/29 and Capital Programme 2026/27 to
2029/30.

·        
approve the ‘Special
Expenses’ budgets, precepts and associated services for
Aylesbury Town, High Wycombe Town and West Wycombe Church Yard
(Appendix 2 and 3).

·        
approve the delegation to Cabinet for
decisions to add up to £100m to the Capital programme, to be
funded by Prudential Borrowing.

·        
approve the updated Council Tax
Reduction Scheme Policy and Equality Impact Assessment (Appendix 4
& 5).

·        
approve the Business Rates
Discretionary Rate Relief Policy (Appendix 6).

·        
approve the Council Tax Discounts and
Premiums Policy (Appendix 7).
 
RESOLVED that:
 

·        
the authority to agree any required
budget changes as a result of the Final Local Government Settlement
be delegated to the s.151 officer in conjunction with the
Leader

·        
a supplementary report, the formal
Council Tax Resolution, will accompany the final Budget to Full
Council.

·        
the Bucks Business Group Response
(Appendix 8) to the Budget be noted.

·        
the Equality Impact assessment for the
proposed budget (Appendix 9) be noted.

purpose:
Feedback report from the Local Government
Association following the Buckinghamshire Council Corporate Peer
Challenge in October 2025.
content:
In October 2025,
Buckinghamshire Council took part in a Corporate Peer Challenge
(CPC). The CPC is a well-established and respected improvement and
assurance tool led by the Local Government Association, which
provided robust, strategic, and credible challenge and support to
councils. Across four days, from 30 September to 3 October 2025, a
team of highly experienced senior local government councillor and
officer peers from other local authorities visited Buckinghamshire
Council to meet with Members, officers, and partners. This was the
first CPC as Buckinghamshire Council and the verbal feedback alone
was a powerful endorsement, with peers calling Buckinghamshire
“one of the best run councils the peer reviewers had ever
visited".
 
The recommendations and
observations set out in the LGA Corporate Peer Challenge feedback
report were advisory. The Council was not required to adopt or
implement them in full. However, all recommendations and comments
would be carefully considered as part of the development of the CPC
action plan, which would be brought to Cabinet for approval. The
action plan would represent the Council’s own agreed response
to the peer team’s findings.
 
RESOLVED that the LGA feedback report recommendations and next
steps be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve recommendations from a Corporate Peer Challenge for Buckinghamshire Council.

purpose:
To recommend the Strategy to Full
Council
content:
The Council was required to
approve its Capital & Investment Strategy on an annual basis.
The Capital & Investment Strategy provided the framework within
which to deliver its Corporate Plan objectives through the
effective investment of its limited capital resources.
 
The key proposed changes
were:
 
• Update the list of
strategies which underpin the Capital Programme to
include
the Economic Growth
Strategy
• Expand references to
Growth Board investment to include leveraging in match
funding from public and private
sector for larger economic development and
regeneration
projects.
• Update references to
Regeneration boards and sub groups to
align with
current governance.
• Updated statistics on
housing and population growth, including reference to
the imposed increase in Housing
Target of 95,000.
• Additional detail added
to the MTFP process to include reference to funding
and Capital
Receipts.
• Reference made to the

residents and businesses to travel while improving travel choices
across the county.

supporting documents be approved for public
consultation.

purpose: To agree the draft budget
content:
The Council was legally
required to publish a balanced budget in February each
year.  The plans set out in this draft
budget had been in development over many months, and subject to
internal check and challenge.  They
would be subject to further scrutiny as part of the upcoming Budget
Scrutiny sessions in week commencing 12th January
2026.
 
In setting this draft budget,
the Council had sought to balance its statutory duties and funding
reductions with residents’ priorities, and this could be seen
in areas of increased investment, including in the continued growth
in funding for Adult Social Care, 
investment to address SEND backlogs; weekly bin collections would
be maintained, planning enforcement was prioritised, and nearly
£220m would be invested in transport and highways.
 
The
financial position for the Council remained challenging with
significant pressures from demand growth, in particular in Social
Care, Home to School Transport, and SEND-related services, in line
with those being experienced nationally. The Council discharged
more than 700 statutory duties, with more than 76% of the
Council’s budget spent in 5 key services: Adult Social Care,
Children’s Services, Home to School Transport and Temporary
Accommodation.
In
addition, this year’s budget included the estimated impacts
of the long-awaited Local Government funding reform. Through the
Fair Funding Review, the Government were redistributing funding to
Councils. As a Council with a relatively high level of Council Tax
income compared to the level of relative modelled need,
Buckinghamshire was set to lose £44.4m of funding. The
Council had been anticipating this reform for a number of years,
and prudently £23.6m of savings towards the impact had
already been made in previous budgets. This budget therefore
included the balance of a further £20.8m of reduced funding
by 2028/29. Transition arrangements were in place to smooth the
impact over 3 years.
The
Council had a strong track record of delivering savings with
£187.3m of income and savings currently delivered since
2020-21. Further savings and additional income of £109.0m
were required to balance the budget to 2028/29. This took the total
value of savings required by 2028/29 to £296m, the equivalent
of 67% of the Council’s first net budget in
2020/21.
By
focussing savings on demand management, invest to save, and
efficiencies rather than cuts, the Council was protecting key
universal services. Within the budget you could also see the
impacts of new Government Policies, in particular for waste and
recycling and national planning policy changes, which the Council
was adapting to and delivering. The Council continued to await the
Government’s delayed announcements on SEND reforms, which was
an area of significant budgetary pressure for the
Council.
The
Fair Funding formula specifically assumed that Council Tax and the
Adult Social Care Precept were maximised. Therefore, the draft
budget was built on the proposed Council Tax base and assumed a
2.99% increase in basic Council Tax and a 2% increase for the Adult
Social Care Precept, giving a total increase of 4.99%. This was the
maximum allowable without triggering a local referendum.
The
draft budget was based on estimates consistent with the Autumn
Budget and Local Government Funding Policy Statement, in particular
the confirmation of assumptions for the Fair Funding review, and
inflation assumptions had been amended in line with the Office of
Budget Responsibility’s updated projections.
The
Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement was published on
17th December 2025 and provided details of provisional central
government funding allocations for 2026/27 to 2028/29, which
alongside the Fair Funding impacts included the new modelled Core
Spending Power (CSP). The modelled core spending power was set to
increase by 8.1% by 28/29 compared to the 25/26 core spending
power. The national average increase in CSP was 15.1%, reflecting
the impact of the Fair Funding impacts on Buckinghamshire and the
movement of funding from the County to other areas via the process
of ‘equalisation’. Buckinghamshire’s increased
spending power was driven entirely by Council Tax and not from any
national increase in funding. Without a 5% per annum increase in
Council Tax, the spending power would in fact reduce by 5%, which
was £30m in Revenue budget terms.
At
the time of publication of the draft budget the Government had made
further grant funding announcements, which the Council would
continue to assess and build into the Final budget. All the funding
announced was ringfenced for specific purposes, and would have
limited scope for local decision making around its
investment.
The
Capital Programme was presented for 4 years for 2026/27 to 2029/30,
with many schemes spanning multiple financial years. In total the
programme included £629m of projects, with £218m being
invested in Transport, including a continued commitment of
£120m Highways investment, alongside increased investment
highways structures and footways, Waste and SEND places, and the
completion of the South East Aylesbury Link Road.
As with previous years, it was
proposed that a recommendation be made to Council in February for
delegation to be given to Cabinet to add up to £100m worth of
schemes to the capital programme, to be funded through prudential
borrowing, subject to a robust business case being approved. This
would enable additional priorities, such as regeneration and
housing projects, to come forward and be added to the capital
programme once positive business cases were fully
developed
 
The final budget would be
reviewed at Cabinet on 10th February and then be
presented for consideration at Full Council on 25th
February. 
 
RESOLVED that
 
1)     
the Draft Revenue Budget and Capital
programme be approved.
2)     
the outcome of the Budget Consultation
(Appendix 1) be noted.
3)     
the Schedule of Fees & Charges for
2026/27 (Appendix 2) be agreed.
4)     
the current risks associated with the
draft budget proposals, in particular the confirmation of the
impact of Fair Funding review on our level of funding from Business
Rates and Grant be noted.
5)     
delegation be sought from Council to
Cabinet for up to £100m of new capital schemes, funded
through Prudential Borrowing, to be added to the Capital programme
where robust financial business cases are made.
6)     
it be noted that a supplementary report,
the formal Council Tax Resolution, will accompany the final Budget
to full Council.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the draft revenue budget and capital programme for the upcoming year, amidst challenges of funding reductions and the need for significant savings.

purpose:
To set Buckinghamshire Council's Council Tax
Base for the following financial year
content:
The Local Authorities
Calculation of Council Tax Base (England) Regulations 2012
prescribed rules for the calculation of the Council Tax base. On an
annual basis, all local authorities were required to calculate a
Council Tax Base which is used to set the level of Council Tax. The
process was governed by the Local Authorities’ (Calculation
of Tax Base) Regulations 1992.
 
In 2026/27, the tax base for
the year was 235,361.84 which was 0.90% higher than 2025/26. The
Collection Rate had increased to 98.5%. 
This included an expected improvement in collection rate of 0.1%
relating to proposed changes to the Council Tax Reduction scheme,
which were subject to consultation and approval by Full Council in
February 2026. The estimated Council Tax surplus was
£6,518,663 as detailed in section 4 of the report.
 
RESOLVED that
i)                   
the Buckinghamshire Council Tax Base of
235,361.84 for the year 2026/27 be approved.
ii)                 
the Buckinghamshire Council’s collection
rate for the year 2026/27 of 98.5% be approved.
iii)               
the estimated surplus as at 31 March 2026 in
relation to Council Tax of £6,518,663 and shared between the Council,
Thames Valley Police and Buckinghamshire Fire & Rescue Service
as detailed in section 4 of the report be
approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve the Council Tax Base, collection rate, and surplus for Buckinghamshire for the year 2026/27.

purpose:
To consider and approve revisions to the Terms
of Reference of the Buckinghamshire Shareholder
Committee.
content:
The Council was a corporate
trustee of several charities, many of which were transferred from
legacy authorities when the unitary authority was created. Trustees
were responsible for compliance with all the legal responsibilities
of a charity, including running the charity and managing its
assets.
 
In August 2024, the Charity
Commission launched a campaign to bring awareness of trustee duties
to local authorities and highlighted failings at other local
authorities.
 
In light of the above and to
enhance the council’s governance arrangements, Cabinet was
recommended that the Buckinghamshire Shareholder Committee’s
Terms of Reference be reviewed to include operational and
governance oversight of the Council owned Trusts.
 
A revised Terms of Reference
was attached at Appendix 1 of the report (proposed additions were
in red text), this delegated decision
making powers to the Committee similar to those which it had
for council owned entities.
 
The reasoning for adding this
to the remit of the Shareholder Committee was to strengthen
existing arrangements, as the Committee had done for council owned
subsidiaries and, in particular to ensure good governance
arrangements exist and that there was improved oversight of risks,
day to day finances, business plans and performance of the Council
owned Trusts.
 
The revised Terms of Reference
envisaged that any proposal to wind up the entities, and to make
any significant operational change to an entity or Trust, or their
assets, would be made as recommendations from the Committee to
Cabinet.
 

RESOLVED that
1)                 
the governance oversight of Council
owned Trusts be incorporated into the Shareholder Committee Terms
of Reference.
2)                 
the
Terms of Reference for the Shareholder Committee as set out in
appendix 1 of the report be adopted with immediate
effect.
3)                 
the
title of the Committee be changed to the Shareholder and Trust
Committee.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to incorporate governance oversight of Council owned Trusts into the Shareholder Committee's Terms of Reference.

purpose:

The Placement & Homes

Appendix 1 of the report) set out a four-year plan to ensure that

accessto theright placement,at theright time,with the right support
– and as close to home as possible. The strategy built on the
Council’s progress in expanding in-house provision, improving
fostering support, and reducing reliance on unregulated and distant
placements. It outlined five strategic objectives, a detailed
implementation plan, and the financial, legal, and corporate
frameworks to ensure delivery.
 
RESOLVED that the Placement and Homes Strategy for Children and
Young People 2026-30 including appendices be approved.

content:
Risk
Management was an integral part of good management and was
essential to the Council’s ability to deliver public services
and as a custodian of public funds. Effective Risk Management could
help all areas of the organisation meet their objectives by
demonstrating compliance, providing assurance, informing decision
making and enabling value for money.
 
Strategic risks were concerned
with the Council’s key priorities as set out in the Corporate
Plan, identifying the principal risks to the achievement of those
and the strategic direction of the Council. These risks could be
immediate impact risks to the organisation’s ability to
continue operating or slow-burning risks that grow and
eventually prevent delivery of
objectives.
 
RESOLVED that the Council’s Risk Management Framework be
noted providing oversight on strategic risks.

purpose:
Use of Conservation Covenants for legally
securing offsite Biodiversity Net Gain habitat banks sites that
geographically span the Buckinghamshire boundary with a
neighbouring local authority
content:
Conservation Covenants were a legal tool,
introduced by the Environment Act 2021, that could be used to
conserve natural or heritage features of land in England. They were
voluntary agreements between a designated Responsible Body and a
landowner to deliver lasting conservation benefits. Each CC
described what the landowner would do to help conserve the land for
public good. They were bespoke legally
binding agreements so they could be tailored to suit different
circumstances. CCs were a helpful tool for BNG in relation to
securing sites for offsite Biodiversity Net Gain. They presented
another opportunity to facilitate the BNG offsite market, which was
important in Buckinghamshire, recognising the scale of housing
growth required. In addition to get onto the national biodiversity
site register (to sell BNG unites to developers), an offsite BNG
site must have been secured using a standalone S106 agreement or a
CC.
 
A CC must be agreed with a designated
Responsible Body who could be a local authority, a public body or
charity, where at least some of its main purposes or functions
relate to conservation; or a private sector organisation, where at
least some of its main activities relate to conservation.
Buckinghamshire became a Responsible Body in May 2024.
 
The Council was able to enter into a CC including land beyond its boundaries
on the basis it was not seeking to exercise a statutory role on
behalf of, or in place of, another (neighbouring) authority.
Therefore, no authority or agreement was needed from the other
Council. A CC was a private, voluntary agreement with a
landowner.
 
The Cabinet Member for Climate Change and
Environment reported that they were looking at Option 3 to secure
offsite BNG sites that geographically cross authority boundaries
with a neighbouring authority. A CC would be a much simpler and
more streamlined way to secure nature related outcomes at these
sites. It would reduce costs by having one agreement instead of two
and be much easier to deliver large landscape scale nature recovery
sites that span the geographic boundary. The only risk would be
managing and enforcing the agreement that would lie outside the
Council boundary. Option 2 was already authorised under delegated
powers. Any revenue cost would be settled by the maintenance fee.
Any fees charged should be set on a full cost recovery basis
including for corporate overheads and cover the full duration of
the agreement.
 
The use of Conservation Covenant in relation
to Option 3 would enable the easier delivery of a landscape scale
habitat bank helping deliver some of the key priorities within the
recently approved Local Nature Recovery Strategy. Importantly, they
also presented opportunities to enable delivery of projects that
supported emerging markets for biodiversity (i.e. mandatory
Biodiversity Net Gain) but also other nature markets, such as
Carbon, Water Quality and Flood Protection. It would also provide
much needed river offsite BNG units, which were currently scarce
nationally in the BNG offsite market.
 
RESOLVED that the
use of Conservation Covenants, in relation to Option 3 (securing
offsite Biodiversity Net Gain Habitat Banks on sites that
geographically cross our boundary with a neighbouring authority),
noting that use of Option 2 is already authorised under delegated
powers, be approved.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to use Conservation Covenants to secure offsite Biodiversity Net Gain Habitat Banks on sites that cross boundaries with a neighboring authority.

purpose:
Seeking permission to conduct a public
consultation on the proposed changes to our Council Tax Reduction
Scheme from 1 April 2026
content:
CTR was a scheme designed to
assist residents on lower incomes or in receipt of certain benefits
in reducing their Council Tax charge. Levels of support for
pension-aged households were determined nationally by the DWP, with
local authorities having had discretion since 2013 to design and
implement their own local schemes to support working age
households. The current harmonised scheme currently provided
support to 13,980 working age households with Council Tax receipts
of £19.7m forgone by the Council per annum.
 
Proposals have therefore been
developed for the introduction of a banded CTR from April 2026 with
a view to:
 
i.                   
Reducing volatility in CTR awards where households
saw changes in income levels, enabling households to better
anticipate levels of support and budget accordingly.
ii.                 
Simplifying calculation of CTR awards, enabling
households to better understand support being provided.
iii.               
Supporting more efficient processing of claims as
the Council was no longer reliant on cross-referencing with
Universal Credit applications made to the DWP – this was
expected to reduced processing times for new applications from 29
days to 10 days.

 
This would target CTR to the
lowest income households more effectively than the current scheme
which would reduce non payment by £0.4 million per annum from
2026/26; reduce the level of savings at which households were no
longer eligible for awards from £16k to £6k from 1
April 2026, which was estimated to result in additional Council Tax
receipts of circa £0.4m and harmonising the levels of income
at which households were no longer eligible for awards over a
three-year period from 1 April 2026, which was estimated to result
in increased Council Tax receipts of circa £0.7m by
2028/29.
 
Overall, the proposed CTR
scheme would therefore increase income available to support local
services by £1.5m, with £0.3m of this sum attributable
to Thames Valley Police and the Buckinghamshire & Milton Keynes
Fire & Rescue Service and £1.2m available to support
Buckinghamshire Council services. In addition, efficiency savings
arising from streamlined administration were expected to deliver a
further £0.2m benefit to Buckinghamshire Council from 2026/27
onwards.
 
In 2026/27, 10,412 or 75% of
households currently in receipt of CTR would see their award either
maintained or increased, reducing the risk of non-payment of
Council Tax within this cohort. 3,500 or 25% of households would
see reduced CTR awards, with 772 or 5.5% of households no longer
meeting the criteria for CTR awards in 2026/27.
 
In order to help households
transition to a banded CTR scheme there would be  in changes in levels of support provided to
individual households, and it was proposed that a form of
transitional protection be provided to those households seeing
larger reductions (i.e. more than £10 per week) in their CTR
awards. There would be year 1 transitional protection so with
households with less than £6,000 this would limit reductions
to £12.50 per week or £650 per annum. Modelling
indicated transitional protection would be provided to 1,720
households at a cost of £0.8m in 2026/27.
 
The proposed scheme would
maintain provision for an exceptional hardship fund, recognising
that there would be individual household circumstances which could
not be fully reflected in the banding scheme assessment. No changes
in administrative arrangements for applications to this fund were
proposed.
 
Of 3,500 households the average
impact would be £538 per annum (£10 per week) in year 1
with the transitional relief rising to £777 per annum
(£15 per week) by year 3. The single largest impact was
£3,661 per annum (£70 per week) which related to a
household in a Band F property previously in receipt of CTR which
was in excess of £6,000. A total of 45 households in Year 1
would see losses of £40 per week which was £2080 per
annum. Households should be enabled to better understand support
being provided and anticipate levels of support and budget
accordingly and it should bolster lower income households reducing
the risk of them falling into arrears.
 
Should proposals ultimately be
adopted as currently drafted this would secure an additional
£1.5m of Council Tax income to the Council by 2028/29, which
would contribute towards meeting the growing costs of
“Critical Five” such as Children’s and
Adults’ Social Care.
 
Public consultation was
required ahead of Cabinet considering proposals in February 2026
which would enable an amended CTR scheme to be adopted from 1 April
2026 (subject to approval by Cabinet and Council). If approved,
consultation would be launched from 17 December 2025.
 
RESOLVED that a six-week consultation from 17 December 2026 with
local taxpayers and other key stakeholders on proposals for
amending the Council Tax Reduction Scheme from 1 April 2026 be
approved.
 
This decision has been
taken under the special urgency procedure. In order to
fulfil the statutory requirement to carry out a consultation, and
to ensure that the public and stakeholders have a proper and
reasonable opportunity to respond, it was determined that the
consultation should start on Wednesday 17 December and run until 2
February. This would then enable the Council to meet the relevant
steps and deadlines towards the setting of council tax. 
Cabinet would meet to consider the outcomes on 10 February 2026 and
would make recommendations to Council on 25 February.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve a consultation on proposed amendments to the Council Tax Reduction Scheme, aiming to target support to low-income households more effectively.

purpose:
To deliver consistency and increased
efficiency of grounds maintenance provision for sites operated by
the Council.
content:
The report was proposing to consolidate all
grounds maintenance activities (currently with idverde , John O’Connor and part of the
in-house North Waste & Street Scene Team ) into a single,
countywide outsourced contract, replacing the current mix of
in-house and multiple external arrangements. This move aimed to
deliver greater consistency, efficiency, and value for money across
council-operated sites, with procurement recommended via the
competitive flexible procedure with preliminary market engagement
(PA23).
 
The new contract, with procurement anticipated
to commence by the end of December 2026, would be output-based to
allow flexibility and potential cost savings, and would require the
TUPE transfer of affected staff. The approach was designed to
ensure service continuity, seek to achieve a reduction to the
current budget costs whilst also addressing legal, financial, and
operational risks associated with the transition.
 
The current contract with idverde had been extended to its legal limit and
would end on 31 December 2026, while the John O’Connor
contract could be extended until 31 March 2028. As idverde cannot be extended further, a new
procurement process was mandatory and must comply with the
Procurement Act 2023 and relevant public contract regulations.
 
The Cabinet Member for Culture and Leisure
reported that the Council currently had a range of arrangements for
grounds maintenance provision: an in-house service covering the
north of the county (part of the North Waste & Street Scene
team) and two contracts for the remainder: idverde (ex Wycombe
area) and John O’Connor (ex-Chiltern and South Bucks area).
Following a review of future options, the recommendation was to
procure a single countywide grounds maintenance contract, with
operational bases located in the north and the south of the county
for efficiency of operations. The procurement team had recommended
that the process was through the Competitive Flexible Procedure
with preliminary market engagement. This route would enable a level
of dialogue with the market which would ensure the Councils future
requirements regarding the potential devolution of sites and their
removal from the contract was fully understood. Also engagement
would look at best use of current facilities and innovation.
 
The contract would be an output-based contract
whereby standards of delivery were specified rather than a
prescribed set of actions. This allowed greater flexibility and
could provide savings should conditions change, and certain
activities become unnecessary i.e. fewer grass cuts during drought
conditions and aligned with industry best practice for a service
contract of this nature.
 
The proposed contract term was five years with
the option for the Council to extend for a period up to a maximum
of 48 months; this was the shortest period that contractors would
be able to recoup their capital outlay for premises and/or
machinery.
 
The Leader made reference to the market and
asked for reassurance that in the procurement exercise local firms
would have a chance to participate. The Head of Neighbourhood
Services reported that through the Competitive Flexible Procedure
they would talk to bidders about whether they could bring in local
small SME’s which was critical for social value for example
some smaller companies would employ their own gravediggers whereas
others would have sub-contractors. However, if the Council had used
open procurement the bidders could submit without dialogue. The
Leader commented on the importance of the local supply chain and
supporting smaller businesses whilst getting best value for the
Council.
 
The Cabinet Member reported that one
representation had been received from a member of staff in the
North In-House Grounds team about their terms and conditions being
protected on transfer to a new contractor. If
Cabinet agreed to the recommendation today, the small number of
staff in this team would move to the new contractor no earlier than
1st January 2027. This transfer would be managed under the Transfer
of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 2006 (TUPE),
which ensured that the Council had specific obligations to protect
permanent staff during this process. Under TUPE, permanent staff
members contractual terms and conditions of employment —such
as pay, hours of work, and annual leave entitlement—would
normally remain the same. However, some non-contractual terms might
need to be reviewed if the incoming service provider was unable to
maintain them.
 
Once the contract award was
confirmed, a full process would begin, including sharing all
relevant information about existing terms and conditions of
employment for employees impacted in this change with the new
service provider. Any proposed changes would be discussed as part
of a formal consultation period. The wellbeing of staff was a top
priority. Any future changes would be communicated clearly and
appropriate support would be provided including guidance throughout
the process.
 
Cabinet Members had considered the
representation.
 
RESOLVED that
 

i)                   
all grounds maintenance activities into a single contract for
Buckinghamshire Council be consolidated.

ii)            
authority be delegated to the Service Director for Neighbourhood
Services, in consultation with the Service Directors for Culture,
Sport and Leisure/Corporate Property and Assets and the Cabinet
Members for Culture and Leisure/Resources/Housing and Regulatory
Services, to conduct a compliant procurement exercise for an
outsourced contract; and upon the conclusion of such competitive
tender process, to award to the preferred tenderer(s) evaluated as
providing the most economically advantageous tender(s) or, in the
event that the preferred tenderer(s) is/are unable or unwilling to
enter into such agreement(s), to award such agreement(s) to the
next willing highest scoring tenderer(s).
topline: The Cabinet has decided to consolidate all grounds maintenance activities into a single contract for Buckinghamshire Council.

content:
Skills Bootcamps offered up to
16 weeks of free, flexible training in high-demand sectors such as
digital, construction, creative industries, green skills, and
leadership. They were designed to align with both national and
local priorities, and they provided residents with a direct pathway
to employment, career progression, or self-employment and include a
guaranteed interview with an employer.
 
Skills Bootcamps formed a key
component of the Government’s Lifetime Skills Guarantee,
aimed at equipping individuals with in-demand skills for sustained
employment. Following the recent transfer of responsibility for
post-19 education and skills from the Department for Education
(DfE) to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), Skills
Bootcamps were now fully managed and funded by the DWP, aligning
delivery more closely with national employment and labour market
priorities.
 
The Bootcamps focused on
vocational skills at levels 2-5 (medium to higher level technical
skills). A key differentiator for the scheme was that, upon
completing the Bootcamp, each learner was guaranteed either an
interview within the relevant sector or confirmation from their
employer that the skills gained were actively being applied in
their role and supporting career progression.  Buckinghamshire Council had been the Accountable
Body responsible for delivery of the programme since July 2023 and
since then the Council has been allocated three ‘waves’
of grant funding, totalling £7.5m.
 
The Leader commented that
national unemployment had increased by 5.1% and with the
Council’s economic strategy it was important to help
Buckinghamshire residents gain the skills they needed. He and one
of his Deputy Leader’s had visited a bootcamp in Iver which
focussed on construction skills and provided two weeks’ worth
of training. There was a high throughput and plenty of job
opportunities in this area.
 
The data from Wave 5
demonstrated a high level of performance, significantly passing the
DWP key performance indicator target of 70%. There were three
stages of milestones: enrolment, completion and job outcomes.
Enrolment performance was 98% against a benchmark of 75%,
Completion performance was 86% against a benchmark of 70-75% and
job outcome was 72% against a benchmark of 70-75%. Following a
targeted marketing campaign 405 participants were enrolled by the
end of the funded year. One learner commented that “The
course has given me the tools and motivation to pursue a new career
path — I feel much more confident now.” There were case
studies included in the report.
 
RESOLVED that the progress be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the progress of the Skills Bootcamps program in Buckinghamshire, showing positive results in enrollment, completion, and job outcomes.

purpose:
To approve a plan to improve Education, Health
and Care plan (EHCP) waiting lists
content:
The report recognised the
implications of the current under performance on Education, Health
and Care Plan (EHCP) assessments for children, young people,
families and schools in Buckinghamshire and proposed additional
investment to improve timeliness, as part of the Council’s
overall improvement programme for SEND.
 
There was a statutory 20-week
deadline from request for an EHC Needs Assessment (EHCNA) to
issuing a final EHC Plan. As of 1st September 2025, there were 1488
children under assessment in Buckinghamshire with 1234 of these
beyond the 20- week deadline. The current average wait of completed
plans was 47 weeks – more than double the target timescale
set out in statute.
 
The report proposed an
investment of a total of £3m to accelerate the EHCP
assessment process and tackle the waiting lists. It was important
to note that an acceleration of EHCP assessments would result in
additional pressure on the High Needs Block to fund the provision
identified in plans, and on the Home to School Transport budget.
These would be built into the emerging Medium Term Financial Plan
2026/27+.
 
The improvement programme was
critical to the longer term sustainability of the system but the
work alone would not tackle the EHCP waiting lists in the short to
medium term. Demand was increasing at a pace that exceeded current
capacity. For example, in September 2025, 121 new EHCNA requests
were received and 66 plans were issued—highlighting the
growing challenge that more cases were entering the system than
were being progressed. On this basis, the Council were unable to
reduce waiting times with the current capacity, and they would in
fact continue to grow without further action. In view of the
ongoing demand, it was recommended that the Council invested as a
priority in additional staffing capacity to accelerate progress for
those families on the waiting list.
 
The Council has engaged with
national government through the Delivering Better Value programme
and had met all the requirements as confirmed by the DfE. 
However, this programme had not met the scale of the rise in
demand.  Furthermore, Government have pushed to an unspecified
date in the future any announcement on SEND funding reforms. 
In this context the Council were taking further action to meet the
rising demand and reduce the EHCP backlog.
 
RESOLVED that £3m be transferred into an earmarked reserve
and that this be invested into reducing the waiting times for
providing EHCP assessments.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to invest £3m to reduce waiting times for EHCP assessments in Buckinghamshire.

purpose:
The Disability Facilities Grant policy has
been updated to provide clarity on the parameters of the policy and
applicants eligibility
content:
Disabled Facilities Grants
(DFG) were delivered by the Grants & Adaptations Team within
the Housing Service, in accordance with the current Housing
Improvement and Adaptations Policy which was adopted in April 2020.
Most of the adaptations that were carried out using DFG funds help
to support residents to live independently for longer at home and
reduce the need for care services or makes lives easier for family
members who care for loved ones. As well as improving independence,
these adaptations were also preventative measures, helping to
reduce hospital admissions due to injuries from falls.
 
The Buckinghamshire Housing
Improvement and Adaptation Policy was a published policy and had
not been updated since its adoption and was currently being applied
to those who approached Buckinghamshire Council to apply for
assistance to keep people safe and independent at home. Since the
last policy was implemented, a new non-statutory guidance on
delivering DFGs was published in 2022, which had driven a review of
the policy to ensure it reflected current best practice.
 
Since 2021-22, the DFG
allocation for Buckinghamshire had been £4.065m annually and
for 2025-26 it was £5.045m. The maximum mandatory DFG was
£30,000, however, as building costs had risen sharply in
recent years and the complexity of need (particularly for disabled
children’s adaptations) had grown, £30,000 was often
inadequate to fully meet complex needs. While demand for DFG
remained high, if expenditure were limited to the mandatory DFG of
£30,000 alone, it was likely that the service would be unable
to spend the full DFG allocation leaving needs of disabled people
unmet.
 
The DFG and Housing Assistance
policy set out how the council would use its discretion to provide
assistance to ensure that needs could be met as well as to ensure
the allocation was fully spent; the objectives of the policy looked
to preventing accidents and poor health and to help people to
remain living independently in their homes for as long as possible.
In addition, DFG funding also supported other related purposes to
meet the policy objectives (for example carrying out essential
repairs and heating improvements). Budget spend was monitored
monthly and priority was given to meeting mandatory adaptation
needs.
 
The current review of the
funding formula (by Government) may result in a smaller allocation
for Buckinghamshire in future years which could impact on the
ability to provide some discretionary assistance.
 
RESOLVED that the Disabled Facilities Grant and Housing
Assistance Policy be approved for adoption.

content:
The Chairman welcomed the
following people to the meeting and thanked Cabinet and Deputy
Cabinet Members and the officers who remained for this
item.

Cllr Michael Bracken,
Deputy Cabinet Member for Planning
Cllr Gary Hall,
Deputy Cabinet Member for Housing
Cllr Peter Brazier,
Cabinet Member for Culture & Leisure

 
During the discussion, the
following points and questions were raised:
 
Leader Portfolio

The Chairman queried
the target of zero square meters on the “Amount of commercial
floorspace generated on enterprise Zones” information which
was provided as a performance indictor for the Leader portfolio.
The Scrutiny Officer would investigate.

                                                                                                         
Action: Sally Moore
Planning
Portfolio

A Member queried the
reporting of planning applications which were decided on time,
pointing out that some applications had been subject to  time extensions. It was explained that a statutory
measure was used for the reported figures. If planning applications
were delayed by the applicant, this could slow the process. The
Chairman stated that it would be helpful to see where any delays
were in the planning approval process. The Corporate Director,
Planning, Growth & Sustainability explained that flexibility
over the end date could be helpful to both parties. Immovable
deadlines could lead to planning refusals, which were not in
anyone’s interest.
Members congratulated
the planning team which had been experiencing very high
workloads.
There was a need for
Members and residents to appreciate the complexity of the planning
process. Planning forums might be useful for some
Members.
The key performance
indictor relating to S106 contributions related to agreements made
by legacy councils and these were potentially at risk of having to
hand the funding back. Nineteen agreements had been at risk and
this figure had now been reduced to two. This figure should reduce
to zero by the time the committee meets again.

 
Housing Portfolio

The Chairman noted
the negative outturn figure for the Council’s Housing
Register (Bucks Home Choice) and asked for the numbers behind the
percentages. The Corporate Director, Planning, Growth &
Sustainability would supply the necessary figures

                                                                                    
Action: Corporate Director,
                                                                                    
Planning, Growth & Sustainability

There was a
discussion on the lack of affordable and key worker housing in
Buckinghamshire, with a Members noting that other councils have
built social housing. The Corporate Director, Planning Growth &
Sustainability noted that the council had previously considered a
motion to investigate building social housing. A decision had been
taken by Cabinet not to pursue a house building
programme.
There was a housing
needs assessment within the draft Buckinghamshire Local Plan and
this will be used as each development site was considered and will
be updated and refreshed regularly. The Corporate Director,
Planning, Growth & Sustainability could provide a link to this
document.

                                                                                      
Action: Corporate Director,
                                                                                      
Planning, Growth & Sustainability

The housing register
applies an allocation policy. Residents categorised into bands A
and B were treated as high priority and were generally housed
within a number of weeks. As there was a mismatch between the
properties available and residents on the register, some residents
will wait have a much longer wait. The Chairman noted that unifying
the county under one system had freed up some properties for those
in the highest need.
A Member noted that a
resident in her ward had been on the housing register for a year
and that the lived experience of people on the list was important
in order to inform policy decisions.
A new housing
allocation policy launched in early 2025 had changed the
eligibility criteria from two to five years’ residency in the
county. The housing team was actively monitoring the register,
which was subject to fluctuations.
The Ukranian guests
housed in Buckinghamshire were mainly staying with families and had
not had an impact on the housing register. Funding from central
government was used to support Ukrainian guests.
The rise in the
number of rough sleepers may have been due to the impact of no
fault evictions. The housing team was monitoring the situation and
had strong links with landlords which would help in understanding
the impact.

 
Culture and Leisure Portfolio

The Cabinet Member
for Culture & Leisure explained that targets were set for each
portfolio by the Corporate Director and the Cabinet Member.
Scrutiny of the progress towards targets took place at Cabinet and
at the relevant Select committees. He agreed that the targets
relating to visits to cultural venues and leisure centres had scope
to be revised upwards.
A decision had been
made that country parks should be cost neutral to the council. In
response to a Member’s question on car parking fees, and car
parking fees, it was explained that there was no data capture of
use by the most vulnerable people of country parks and that a
targeted approach was taken to ensure accessibility
Buckinghamshire
Archives had used social media to promote Buckinghamshire History
Festival and members of the public had been given tours of archive.
Once Buckinghamshire Archives has been relocated to its new
premises in High Wycombe, it will be more accessible. A Member
suggested that local libraries could be used to promote the
Archives Service and the Cabinet Member for Culture & Leisure
agreed that this was a good suggestion.
The “Percentage
of library enquiries resolved” indictor described customer
queries which were answered at the library and did not need to be
escalated to a service.

 
The Chairman thanked the
Cabinet Members and officers for their contributions on this
item.

purpose:
Quarterly report to Cabinet on our Corporate
performance indicators.
content:
The performance report provided
details of the key performance measures reported through the
corporate performance framework for 2025/26. Latest performance
outturns and targets were reported alongside trend and benchmarking
information, where available. Commentary was provided for each
indicator explaining what was being measured, explaining the
narrative behind each outturn and detailing improvement
actions.
 
Within the performance report,
outturns which were performing at or better than target were
classified as Green, those which were within 5% of the target were
Amber and those which were more than 5% of the target were Red. At
the end of quarter 2, 66 indicators had outturns reported with a
Red, Amber or Green status. Of these, 44 were Green (67%), 6 were
Amber (9%) and 16 were Red (24%). This compared with 64 indicators
with outturns reported in quarter 1, and of these, 47 were Green
(73%), 3 were Amber (5%) and 14 were Red (22%).
 
RESOLVED the Council’s performance be noted including the
action taken to improve performance where required.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the Council's performance report for 2025/26 and take action to improve performance where necessary.

The report detailed further

purpose:
To endorse the Director of Public Health
Annual Report.
content:
Each year every Director of
Public Health in England must produce a statutory annual report on
the health of their population. The Buckinghamshire Director of
Public Health Annual Report (DPHAR) 2025 focussed on the theme of
“Tomorrow’s health and wellbeing”. This theme was
selected in light of population changes
in Buckinghamshire, both due to the population aging and new
housing, plus the significant health challenges impacting local
services and productivity. It explored how the health and wellbeing
of Buckinghamshire residents would change in the next 20 years. The
impact of health inequalities and their link to the building blocks
of health demonstrate the importance of targeting collective effort
to areas and communities with the greatest need and the most to
gain. The recommendations from the report were broad and did not
just sit with Buckinghamshire Council, but required the input of
several different organisations, often working together in
partnership.
 
RESOLVED that the report be endorsed and published.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to endorse and publish the Buckinghamshire Director of Public Health Annual Report 2025, focusing on 'Tomorrow's health and wellbeing'.

purpose: Quarterly report
content:
The report set out the forecast
Revenue and Capital outturn position for Buckinghamshire Council
for the financial year 2025/26 as at Quarter 2. Overall, the
forecast revenue outturn was a balanced position. The Council
continued to experience significant financial pressures from
increases in demand and complexity of need in the key services of
Adult Social Care, Children’s Social Care, Temporary
Accommodation, Home to School Transport and High Needs budgets
within the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG). The forecast revenue
outturn position at Quarter 2 within Portfolios was an adverse
variance of £2.1m (0.4% of Portfolio budgets), compared with
£5.5m reported in Q1. This improvement was due to the success
of strong management action and political oversight with particular
focus on challenge in high-risk areas.
 
The pressures in the forecast
were in Children’s Social Care (£2.8m), Parking income
(£0.8m), Home to School Transport (£1.1m) and Temporary
Accommodation (£0.8m), offset by £0.6m underspend from
vacancies in Parking staffing budgets, £0.7m additional
planning income and £0.8m managed underspend from vacancies
in Resources and Health and Wellbeing. A balanced position overall
was due to a favourable variance in Corporate and Funding
budgets.
 
The Dedicated Schools Grant
budget has been set with a deficit of £22.9m. Currently the
forecast position was within budget, however there was continued
high demand for EHC Needs Assessments and a range of measures were
being considered to tackle the delays in waiting times. There was a
risk of increased demand impacting adversely on the financial
position in the second half of the year. The balance on the DSG
deficit reserve at the beginning of the year was £24.5m with
a forecast closing balance of £47.4m.
 
The forecast position on
capital budgets was £173.7m, which matched the current budget
after reprofiling to reflect an updated and prudent view on the
delivery of projects. The budget included an approved savings
programme of £115.6m over 3 years, with £76.9m to be
delivered in 2025/26. Delivery of savings for 2025/26 was currently
forecast at 0.9% above target with a total £0.7m of savings
above budget. Actions would continue to be required to closely
manage the in-year financial position.
 
RESOLVED that the report be noted.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the forecast revenue and capital outturn position for Buckinghamshire Council for the financial year 2025/26.

purpose:
To agree marketing and disposal of 5
sites
content:
This report sought to authorise
the Corporate Director for Resources, in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Resources, to proceed with a disposal programme
of five sites, all identified as being surplus Council owned
assets. The assets were spread across the County – two in
High Wycombe, one in Aylesbury, with the others being in Wing and
Winslow. All bar one of the sites were already identified for
disposal in the current MTFP. The exception was previously
allocated to a development project with a public sector partner,
but this transaction had recently fallen away. This site
was  vacant, non-revenue generating and
available for immediate disposal.
 
The marketing strategy for each
site was to conduct an open market campaign seeking conditional and
unconditional offers. The objective was to attract a broad range of
bids for each of the sites. These can then be evaluated to
determine which proposal best met the Council’s overall
objectives including financial, and contribution to both the
economic growth prospects and social benefits to the area. Disposal
of these sites for housing would also comply with Priority 3 of the
Buckinghamshire Housing Strategy to “explore the use of local
authority assets and resources for the purposes of delivering
additional new housing.
 
The five properties
were:-
i.                   
Orchard House and Courtyard site, both in High
Wycombe (to be marketed at the same time).
ii.                 
Thame Road, Aylesbury, adjoining Aylesbury
College.
iii.               
Former Highway Depot site, Wing.
iv.               
Four single dwelling plots on Oak Way,
Winslow.
 
RESOLVED that with regard to all of the sites listed at
paragraph 3.2, that the  Corporate
Director for Resources be authorised in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Resources to:
 
• Market the sites to achieve the best consideration under
Section 123 of the Local Government Act 1972.
• Appoint a marketing agent to secure bids for the disposal
of the sites.
• Approve a disposal budget to cover marketing, due
diligence and legal costs as set out in the Confidential Annex of
the report.
• Implement the Council’s communication
plan.
• Negotiate draft heads of terms with preferred purchasers
and instruct legal to prepare all the necessary legal
documentation, agreements including service of any notices and/or
submission of any applications required for the sale of these
properties.
• With regard to the Winslow site only, in the event of no
offers for all four plots being received, plots to be lotted and
considered for individual sale.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to authorize the disposal of five surplus Council owned assets for housing development.

purpose:
Seeking amendment to the Cabinet decision of
9th November 2021 – Land Acquisition, Compulsory Purchase
Order and Side Roads Order
content:
Seeking amendment to the Cabinet decision of
9th November 2021 – Land Acquisition, Compulsory Purchase
Order and Side Roads Order

The Princes Risborough Southern
Road Link (PRSRL) was currently stalled, and this report set out
the current position and that the Council could no longer carry out
the construction of the PRSRL. It was now anticipated that the road
would be constructed by developers wishing to progress housing
development in the Expansion Area. This report set out the
implications of not pursuing the planning application, the existing
blight risk, and the current challenges relating to the Princes
Risborough Expansion Area. The Council had been unable to secure
the additional funding to meet the full cost of delivery of the
scheme and consequently could not pursue a Compulsory Purchase
Order for the necessary land, or
contractually commit to the construction of the road.
 
Due to significant price
inflation, in late 2021 a Cabinet paper set out that the Council
would be unable to deliver the road. All expenditure on the project
was halted by the Council in early 2023 (with some legal costs
ongoing) and staff reallocated to other work. Protracted
negotiations with developers of the PREA took place from Summer
2023 until Autumn 2024 to attempt to include delivery of the road
as part of anticipated planning applications. Unfortunately, it was
confirmed by developers in late 2024 that this would not happen
in the near future.
 
A representation had been
received from a member of the public which was taken into account by Cabinet Members before the
decision was taken.
 
RESOLVED that
 

·        
no further steps be taken to pursue the planning
application for the Princes Risborough Southern Link Road scheme
and cease all negotiations with Network Rail.

·        
no further steps be taken under the Cabinet
decision of 9th November 2021 in respect of PRSRL– Land
Acquisition, Compulsory Purchase Order and Side Roads Order”
as detailed in Confidential Appendix A of the report

·        
use of existing capital budget of
£1,467,697 be approved for ongoing work and that this be
delegated to the Corporate Director for Planning, Growth and
Sustainability (PG&S) to:

o Take all necessary steps to make the Little Kimble
Cottages safe and secure. Pursue further options utilising existing
budget

o Continue to fund analysis of the Buckinghamshire
Transport model against the whole PREA.

o Make budget adjustments to the approved use of
existing capital budget of £1,467,697 for ongoing work
including managing existing assets, establishing necessary further
highways modelling work, and offsetting potential risks as set out
in Confidential Appendix A of the report.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to abandon the Princes Risborough Southern Road Link project due to funding challenges and inability to secure necessary land.

purpose:
Cabinet to receive an update on the progress
with delivering the Parking Strategy and agree to approve the
market testing of the parking enforcement service.
content:
The report set out the progress
that had been made following the adoption of the Council’s
Parking Strategy in February 2024 and provided an update on the
progress for the outsourcing of parking enforcement services. The
parking enforcement service had never achieved optimum performance
due to significant resourcing and operational challenges, which had
significantly impacted on parking compliance as well as creating an
inability for targeted and intelligent deployment. The current
model for delivering parking enforcement services, with its
continued resourcing challenges, was not sustainable and created
financial and reputational risks to the Council.
 
The model for parking services
had been reviewed including outsourcing of the enforcement
functions and work had been undertaken to prepare for a tender
process which would commence in November 2025. The proposed
outsourced model would move the service to an ‘intelligence
led, compliance based’ service that sought to deliver a
minimum of 90% compliance with the parking regulations and embraced
technology and innovation. The proposed model should provide well
managed, efficient, resilient and cost[1]effective parking services, which would
increase prosperity and improve the environment. The current
programme was to award contract to the preferred bidder in January
2026 and for implementation in June 2026, allowing for TUPE and
mobilisation.
 
RESOLVED that
 
1.
the progress made with the implementation of the parking strategy
be noted.
2.
the high-level specification for the outsourcing of parking
enforcement services as set out in the report be
approved.
3.
approval of the final specification for outsourcing of parking
enforcement services be delegated to the Corporate Director for
Communities, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for
Communities.
4.
the market testing for parking enforcement services be
approved.
5.
the timetable for the procurement exercise and contract award be
noted.
6.
the award of contract to the preferred bidder following evaluation,
subject to being within the approved budget, be delegated to the
Corporate Director for Communities, in consultation with the
Cabinet Member for Communities.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to outsource parking enforcement services to improve compliance and address resourcing challenges.
